items.name: Pulse Raiser
items.setup: Open floor away from the climbing wall's fall zones.
steps: 2–5 minutes of jogging, skipping, star jumps or high knees.
Build the pace gradually until everyone is warm and slightly out of breath.
Finish standing still so the group is ready to listen.
items.why: BMC's FUNdamentals notes build a climbing warm-up in three parts: pulse raiser, joint rotation, then easy climbing. Raising heart rate and body temperature first prepares muscles and gets attention on you.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3) to Ages 4–6: tell a story (run from the rain, jump the puddles). Ages 6–9 and Ages 9–12: follow-the-leader on separate lanes. Ages 12+ (training) and Ages 14+ (competitive): athlete-led.
items.risk: Keep running lanes clear of bags, ropes and the landing zones under climbers.

items.name: Joint Circles
items.setup: Group in a circle on the mats.
steps: Circle the wrists, elbows, shoulders, hips, knees and ankles about 10 times each way.
Open and close the fingers, then gentle finger and forearm stretches.
Finish with arm swings and leg swings.
items.why: Joint rotation is the second step of the BMC warm-up model; it takes joints through the ranges climbing will ask for.
items.variations: Little: name each move after an animal (owl neck, flamingo ankle). Kids: a climber counts. Teens: their own routine, checked by you.
items.risk: Keep stretches gentle and pain-free; growing joints don't need forced range.

items.name: Easy Climbing Build-Up
items.setup: 3–6 problems or routes well below each climber's limit.
steps: Start on big holds and easy angles.
Each climb a little harder or steeper than the last.
Only move to small holds after several easy climbs.
items.why: The third part of the BMC warm-up: easy climbing prepares fingers and tendons and grooves movement before harder efforts.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: two easy climbs with a coach. Ages 6–9: one-color circuit. Ages 9–12 and older: build to about two grades below their max.
items.risk: Small crimps and steep pulls only after the build-up; finger loading is the main injury risk for young climbers.

items.name: Animal Walks
items.setup: A path across the mats, optionally with soft blocks to crawl over.
steps: Show one animal at a time: bear crawl, crab walk, frog jump, inchworm, flamingo stand.
Kids travel the path as that animal.
Change the animal each lap.
items.why: Crawling and quadruped movement build shoulder and core strength and coordination the wall will use, while feeling like play.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3): parent crawls beside the child. Ages 3–4 and Ages 4–6: kids pick the next animal. Ages 6–9: try to beat their own time.
items.risk: One direction of travel to avoid head bumps; keep the path off the landing zones.

items.name: Climber-Led Warm-Up
items.setup: Rotate a different climber as leader each week.
steps: The leader runs pulse raiser, joint circles and an easy climbing build-up.
You watch and step in only if a part is missing.
The group gives the leader one compliment.
items.why: Handing over the warm-up builds autonomy and makes the warm-up structure a habit they keep outside class.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: leader picks from a card of options. Ages 12+ (training): leader designs it. Ages 14+ (competitive): each athlete runs a personal, specific warm-up.
items.risk: Check the leader includes easy climbing before small holds.

items.name: Workout Dice
items.setup: Two blank dice: one with exercises (push-up, jumping jack, squat, plank), one with numbers.
steps: Each climber rolls both dice.
Everyone does that exercise that many times.
Pass the dice to the next roller.
items.why: Chance keeps it exciting and gives every kid a turn as leader.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: easy moves, small numbers. Ages 9–12 and Ages 12+ (training): add climbing-specific moves such as scapular shrugs.
items.risk: Keep numbers modest; no maximal efforts in a warm-up.

items.name: Alphabet Exercise
items.setup: A chart assigning a stretch or exercise to every letter.
steps: Circle up; each person says their name.
Each person spells their name by doing the move for each letter, with the group joining in.
items.why: A name game and a warm-up at once, useful on the first day.
items.variations: Shorter names or first initial only for younger kids; teens can spell a climbing word instead.
items.risk: Choose low-load moves for the letter chart.

items.name: Look Up, Look Down
items.setup: Tight standing circle.
steps: On “look down” everyone looks at their toes.
On “look up” everyone looks straight at someone in the circle.
If two people meet eyes, they high-five and swap places. Count those matches.
The group tries to get fewer matches on the next round.
items.why: A quick energizer. The group works together to make fewer matches each round.
items.variations: Split groups bigger than about 20 into smaller circles.
items.risk: Low risk; play on flat floor away from the wall.

items.name: Joe and the Button Factory
items.setup: Group standing where all can see you.
steps: Sing the verse: Joe's boss asks him to turn a button with one hand.
Each verse adds a body part (other hand, a foot, the head).
Finish with everything moving.
items.why: Repetition with one change per round fits how young children learn; it gets bodies moving and ears listening.
items.variations: Ages 3–4: slower, with you modelling. Ages 6–9: a kid leads.
items.risk: Leave space between kids for moving arms.

items.name: Nailed It
items.setup: A line on the mat; climbers start one step back.
steps: Jump to the line and sink into bent knees to absorb the landing.
Hold the balance for a second.
Each round start one step farther back. A wobble means reset and try that distance again.
items.why: Practising soft, bent-knee landings on the floor prepares for bouldering falls and for dynamic moves.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: frog jumps onto a mat spot. Ages 6–9: add a turn in the air. Teens: jump from a low box.
items.risk: Land on two feet with bent knees; no locked knees and no landing on hands.

items.name: Learn to Fall
items.setup: Clear landing zone on the bouldering mats; demo first.
steps: Demo on the floor: land on the feet, bend the knees, sit back, roll onto the back, arms in like a turtle.
Practise from standing, then from the lowest holds.
Progress to about halfway up the wall when the landing is controlled.
items.why: Falling is part of climbing; a rehearsed landing reduces injury risk and fear, which frees kids to try harder moves.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3): parent holds hands and they ‘fall like a leaf’ together from the first hold. Ages 3–4: Turtle Tuck story. Ages 6–9 through Ages 14+ (competitive): add falls from awkward positions and sideways.
items.risk: Check the landing zone is clear before every fall; no arms reaching back to catch the fall; only one climber per fall zone.

items.name: Buddies Up
items.setup: Large open area.
steps: On “go” everyone finds a partner of similar size.
Call challenges for pairs (back to back, high five, sit down together).
Call a new pairing to mix the group.
items.why: Fast partner-finding sets up belay and buddy-check pairs for the rest of class.
items.variations: Use it to form climbing pairs at the end.
items.risk: Walking only if space is tight.

items.name: O Captain, My Captain
items.setup: Large area; one end is the bow, the other the stern.
steps: The captain calls commands: bow, stern, hit the deck, man overboard.
Players act them out.
If the group misses a call, practise that one again.
items.why: Command-and-response games train listening, which you need for climbing commands.
items.variations: Add climbing commands as ship orders (“On belay!”).
items.risk: Hit the deck onto mats only.

items.name: Lava Crossing
items.setup: Foam pads laid out from a start pad to an end pad.
steps: The team must get everyone from the start pad to the end pad.
Only the pads count as ground; the floor is lava.
Remove a pad when nobody is touching it.
items.why: A team problem with no single answer: planning, communication and including everyone.
items.variations: Fewer pads or a time limit for older groups.
items.risk: Use low, stable pads; no stacking.

items.name: Nitro Crossing
items.setup: Two pads as islands and a hanging rope swing between them (only where your gym has a rigged swing).
steps: Everyone starts on one island.
Use the swing to move everyone to the other island without touching the floor. One person on the swing at a time.
Optional: carry a bean bag across too.
items.why: A classic adventure-education team challenge: planning, trust and encouragement.
items.variations: Add a time limit or a no-talking round.
items.risk: Only with a swing rigged and checked by staff; one person on the swing at a time; spotters at each island.

items.name: Parachute Games
items.setup: A play parachute; kids spaced evenly around the edge.
steps: Mushroom: pull it taut low, then all lift on a signal so it balloons up.
Matching Colors: give each child a color; when you call it, they run under to the other side before it comes down.
items.why: Shared rhythm and turn-taking for the youngest groups; great for a Review & Play day.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3): parents hold the edge with the child.
items.risk: Only one color crossing at a time to avoid collisions.

items.name: Bosu Balance
items.setup: A Bosu ball (or balance board) on a mat; groups of 2–3.
steps: Each person balances on the Bosu for a set count, in a fixed order.
Toss a ball while you balance, then step off and the next person steps on.
Balance board version: the group tries to solve the ball puzzle in the center.
items.why: Trains the balance and core control used to stay over the feet on the wall; also a good belay-line activity.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: hold a coach's hand. Older: catch while balancing on one foot.
items.risk: On a mat, away from the wall and its fall zones; a spotter beside the Bosu.

items.name: Pick and Choose
items.setup: Buckets at different distances and a pile of tennis balls.
steps: For two minutes the group counts how many throws land in a bucket.
Talk about what to try next, then try to beat the group's last count.
items.why: A team-total goal rather than individual ranking, which suits a mastery climate.
items.variations: Each person takes at least one throw.
items.risk: Throw toward the buckets only, away from climbers.

items.name: Animal Name Game
items.setup: Seated circle, coaches included.
steps: Say your name, an animal starting with the same letter, and an action.
Each person repeats the names and actions before theirs.
items.why: Learning names on day one builds belonging, which keeps kids coming back.
items.variations: Teens: use a climbing move instead of an animal.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Adjective Name Game
items.setup: Seated circle.
steps: Each person says an adjective starting with their first letter plus their name (Crimpy Cam).
Go around again. The group keeps going until everyone can say the names.
items.why: Fast name learning for new groups.
items.variations: Climbing adjectives only for older kids.
items.risk: Low risk; steer away from teasing adjectives.

items.name: Move If…
items.setup: A circle of place markers, one for every person. The caller stands with the group and the caller role moves in a set order.
steps: The caller says “Move if…” plus something true for them (you have a dog).
Everyone it is true for moves to a different marker. There is a marker for every person.
The next person in the circle becomes the caller.
items.why: Kids learn what they have in common while moving, and everyone keeps a place.
items.variations: Climbing prompts: move if you've heel hooked.
items.risk: Walking only; markers flat on the floor.

items.name: Desert Island
items.setup: Small seated group.
steps: You're stuck on a desert island for a year: pick one book and one luxury item.
Each person shares and explains.
items.why: A low-pressure get-to-know-you for older groups or belay-line downtime.
items.variations: Climbing twist: one route you'd bring.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Question Web
items.setup: Standing circle and a spool of string.
steps: Hold the end, ask someone across the circle a question, pass the spool.
They answer, hold the string, ask and pass on.
End by looking at the web: everyone is connected.
items.why: Visual reminder that the group is a team; good first-week closer.
items.variations: Questions about climbing goals for older groups.
items.risk: Hold string at waist height.

items.name: Two Truths and a Lie
items.setup: Small group, or a belay line.
steps: One person says two true things and one untrue thing about themselves.
The others guess which is the lie.
items.why: Gets kids talking while waiting for a rope, so nobody wanders.
items.variations: Write them down first (Fact or Fiction).
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Interview
items.setup: Pairs.
steps: Three minutes to find three interesting facts about your partner.
Introduce your partner to the group.
items.why: Builds the trust belay partners need.
items.variations: Add one climbing goal per person.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: 20 Questions
items.setup: Belay line or waiting area.
steps: One person thinks of a person, place or thing.
Others ask up to 20 yes-or-no questions to guess it.
items.why: Keeps waiting climbers engaged and close by.
items.variations: Climbing-only answers (a hold type, a knot).
items.risk: Keep the line out of the belayer's way.

items.name: Lava Obstacle Course
items.setup: Course of crash pads, volumes, ropes on the floor and a low traverse.
steps: The floor is lava for the whole course.
Everyone travels from the start to the finish, ‘Party Island’.
Time it for a variation.
items.why: Mixes balance, crawling and low climbing in one flow.
items.variations: Ages 3–4: coach walks beside. Ages 9–12: timed laps to beat their own time.
items.risk: Keep volumes low, pads butted together with no gaps, one-way traffic.

items.name: Hot Lava
aka: The Floor Is Lava (on the wall)
items.setup: Kids start on the ground near a low traverse wall.
steps: Call “The ground is hot lava!” and kids get on the wall.
Or call “The wall is hot lava!” and they step down to the mat.
Mark ‘islands’ where tired climbers can step down.
items.why: Short, playful traverse time with a clear signal to follow.
items.variations: Ages 3–4: islands every few steps. Ages 6–9: stay on for longer counts.
items.risk: Feet below about knee height for the youngest; step down, don't jump.

items.name: Freeze Traverse
items.setup: Everyone spaced out on a traverse; music optional.
steps: Climbers move along the wall.
On “Freeze!” (or when the music stops) everyone stops wherever they are.
Hold the freeze, then move again.
items.why: Freezing in odd positions teaches balance and finding rest stances.
items.variations: Ages 3–4: a stop-and-go story. Ages 6–9: freeze with straight arms. Ages 12+ (training): freeze then shake out each hand.
items.risk: Space climbers so nobody is directly above or below another.

items.name: 10 Seconds
items.setup: Bounded section of wall.
steps: Count down from five while kids find a spot on the wall.
On “Freeze!” they hold on and you count 10.
Coach straight arms and a light grip during the hold.
items.why: Short holds make straight arms and relaxed grip noticeable.
items.variations: Add foot-position calls (see Quick Step).
items.risk: Low holds; counts short for little ones.

items.name: Simon Says
items.setup: Bouldering wall with lots of holds; kids start with hands and feet on.
steps: Simon calls moves: “Simon says outside flag with your left foot.”
Move only when Simon says.
A missed call means try that move again. Everyone stays on the wall.
items.why: Reviews technique words under light pressure; kids show you what they know, each on their own holds.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: simple calls (touch a blue hold). Ages 9–12 and Ages 12+ (training): technique calls (drop knee, gaston).
items.risk: Low wall; spread climbers so falls land clear of each other.

items.name: Squish
items.setup: Climbers on a line in front of a traverse.
steps: Only when you say “Squish” do climbers go to the wall.
Call techniques: match on a jug, switch feet, smear, sidepull, backstep, drop knee.
A missed call means try it again. Everyone stays in.
items.why: A listening check and a quick read of what each climber already knows.
items.variations: Fewer calls and big holds for younger kids; heel hooks and drop knees for older.
items.risk: Wait for “Squish” so nobody runs into the wall; spacing between climbers.

items.name: Animal Crossing
items.setup: Easy traverse or low wall.
steps: Pick an animal (bear, monkey, frog, sloth).
Climb or traverse the way that animal would move.
Next climber picks a new animal.
items.why: Animal images give young kids a movement idea without technical words.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3): parent and child pick together. Ages 6–9: guess the animal from the movement.
items.risk: Frog jumps only on the mat, not off the wall.

items.name: Animal Habitats
items.setup: Split a low bouldering wall into air, land and water sections.
steps: Call an animal.
Kids move to the right section of the wall for where it lives.
items.why: Gets kids moving across the wall and thinking at the same time.
items.variations: Add a second rule (move only on blue holds).
items.risk: Kids step down to move between sections rather than crowding.

items.name: Rescue Mission
items.setup: Stuffed animals clipped with a sling to holds on the wall.
steps: Tell the story: the animals are stuck and need rescuing.
Each child climbs to an animal and brings it down.
items.why: A clear, kind goal pulls nervous kids up the wall a little higher each time.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3): parent spots and cheers. Ages 4–6: on top rope. Whole-group version for a celebration day.
items.risk: Place animals at a height that fits each child; climb down or lower, no jumping holding the toy.

items.name: Fuzz-Ball Search
items.setup: Hide pom-poms or small toys on holds.
steps: Kids climb or traverse to find one.
Rule: both feet on the wall when you grab it.
Downclimb once you have it; one find per climb.
items.why: Eldo recommends it to reduce fear and add playfulness; the downclimb rule teaches balance.
items.variations: The class collects every pom-pom into one bucket on a celebration day.
items.risk: Use objects too big to swallow for under-4s; no food rewards if allergies are possible.

items.name: Puzzle Hunt
items.setup: A large-piece puzzle, pieces hidden on the wall (some low, some high).
steps: Kids climb to collect pieces.
The group assembles the puzzle together.
items.why: A shared goal motivates kids to climb higher without ranking anyone.
items.variations: Fewer, bigger pieces for little ones; hard pieces up high for Ages 9–12.
items.risk: High pieces only on top rope.

items.name: Climbing Hide and Seek
items.setup: Slips of paper hidden high enough that players must climb to see them.
steps: Players look and climb to find the papers, each on their own part of the wall.
Each finder brings one down and reads the word.
Keep going until the papers are found.
items.why: Gets kids scanning the wall, a first step toward reading routes.
items.variations: Put a climbing word on each slip to teach vocabulary.
items.risk: Hide within reach of easy holds; top rope for anything high.

items.name: Duck Hunt
items.setup: A rubber duck; bouldering area.
steps: Some climbers hide the duck on the wall while the rest don't look.
The others climb to find it.
Finders become the next hiders.
items.why: Strategy and scanning the wall, as a relaxed cool-down.
items.variations: Hide it only on a certain wall angle.
items.risk: Hiders stay within easy reach; no climbing over others.

items.name: Dress-Up
items.setup: Hats, glasses, gloves or shirts hung on holds along a traverse or route.
steps: Climb to an item and put it on while on the wall.
Save the hardest items (a shirt) for the top.
items.why: Putting something on while climbing forces kids to find rest positions and balance on one hand.
items.variations: Older kids: time your own trip along the traverse and try to beat that time.
items.risk: Tuck away anything dangling so it can't snag on holds or a rope.

items.name: Tootsie Traverse
items.setup: A treat or sticker on many holds. One climber on the traverse at a time.
steps: The climber traverses, collecting items, then steps down.
The next climber starts only after the wall is clear. Keep climbers spaced apart.
items.why: Collecting items adds a reason to keep moving, with one climber on the wall at a time.
items.variations: Use stickers instead of candy.
items.risk: Stickers avoid allergy issues. Wait until the traverse is clear before the next climber starts.

items.name: Hula Hoop Traverse
items.setup: Hula hoops held by coaches or hung on the wall along a traverse.
steps: Kids traverse and pass through each hoop without stepping off.
items.why: Forces kids to bring the body in close and move hips around obstacles.
items.variations: Smaller hoops or more of them for older kids.
items.risk: Coaches holding hoops stand clear of the climber's fall line.

items.name: Climbing Limbo
items.setup: A pool noodle or stick held across a traverse.
steps: Each player traverses and goes under the stick while staying on the wall.
Lower the stick each round.
items.why: Teaches low, wide body positions and hip flexibility.
items.variations: Over-and-under version: stick high for some rounds.
items.risk: Use a soft noodle; holder stands clear.

items.name: Wake-Up Wall
items.setup: Climbers lie on the mat, heads near the wall, an arm's length apart.
steps: Tell a story. On the trigger word (“wake up!”) everyone gets onto their own part of the wall.
The group adds one sentence, then climbs again.
items.why: A story game that holds young kids' attention, each climber on their own lane.
items.variations: Change the trigger word each round.
items.risk: Arm's-length spacing; only low holds.

items.name: Swinging Monkeys
items.setup: Kids on a low wall, spaced apart.
steps: Sing: “Five little monkeys climbing on the wall…”
Everyone tries to stay on for the verse.
Come down when you need to, rest, and cheer the next verse.
items.why: A song plus a reason to stay on the wall; endurance for little ones, with no catching.
items.variations: Count the monkeys down each verse.
items.risk: Feet stay low. Step down when tired; do not jump.

items.name: Monkeys and Bananas
items.setup: Each climber has their own lane on a low wall. The coach calls the words.
steps: On “Monkeys get on the wall!” everyone finds their own spot to hang.
The coach says “Monkeys!” and everyone answers “Bananas!”
On “Monkeys off the wall!” everyone steps down, rests, and gets back on for the next call.
items.why: Rewards relaxed straight-arm hanging and quiet movement.
items.variations: Let a climber take a turn as the caller, in a set order.
items.risk: Callers stay on the mat, clear of the fall zone.

items.name: High-Five the Star
items.setup: A star sticker or bell at a different height for each child.
steps: Each child climbs to tap the star or ring the bell.
Move it a little higher only if the child wants.
items.why: A visible, chosen target gives young kids control over how brave to be.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3): parent places the star. Ages 4–6: bell on top rope.
items.risk: Bouldering targets stay within a short step of the mat for under-4s.

items.name: Color Detective
items.setup: Low wall with clearly colored holds.
steps: Call a color; kids find and touch a hold of that color.
Then hands only on that color for a short climb.
items.why: Color-following is the first step to climbing a set route.
items.variations: Add a foot rule (feet anywhere) for Ages 4–6.
items.risk: Keep climbs low; one child per section.

items.name: Mirror Me
items.setup: Pairs or small groups on an easy section.
steps: One climber does a short sequence.
The others copy it exactly.
Add a harder move each round; swap leaders.
items.why: Watching and copying builds a movement library; Momentum's Mirror Match adds watching a partner closely and repeating their beta.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3): the child copies the parent, then leads. Ages 9–12 and older: add one harder move each round and swap leaders.
items.risk: Copy only moves the copier can reverse or step down from.

items.name: Octopus
items.setup: A jug and plenty of footholds around it.
steps: Hold the jug (or a good stance).
Touch as many different holds as you can with your feet without letting go.
Count one for each hold you touch.
items.why: Builds reach, flexibility and foot awareness on a small piece of wall.
items.variations: How Many Holds: from a four-point stance, test reach one limb at a time.
items.risk: Low on the wall; step down when tired.

items.name: Blindfold Climbing
items.setup: Pairs; easy top-rope route or low traverse; a blindfold.
steps: The climber is blindfolded.
The partner guides with words only.
Switch roles.
items.why: Teaches climbing by feel, clear communication and trust.
items.variations: Mark how far each pair gets, then try to pass their own mark. The guide stays on the ground.
items.risk: On top rope or very low; partner calls holds clearly and stops the climb if the climber drifts.

items.name: Climbing Communication Breakdown
items.setup: Three roles: a blindfolded climber, a silent mime who can see, and a speaker who can't see the wall.
steps: The mime gestures directions to the speaker.
The speaker tells the climber.
Rotate roles.
items.why: Shows how quickly messages break down; reinforces clear commands.
items.variations: Limit the speaker to climbing vocabulary.
items.risk: Top rope with an attentive belayer or a very low traverse.

items.name: Narrated Climb
items.setup: A climber and a narrator on the ground.
steps: The climber moves only on the narrator's instructions.
The narrator must use climbing words (hold names and techniques).
items.why: Tests and grows vocabulary in context.
items.variations: Blindfold the climber for older kids.
items.risk: Easy terrain; narrator stops the climber if unsure.

items.name: Take Away
items.setup: A traverse or route.
steps: Climb it once.
Remove one hold (tape it off) and climb again.
Keep removing holds until it can't be climbed.
items.why: Each removal forces a new solution; a great strength and footwork challenge.
items.variations: Team version: each climber removes one hold for the next.
items.risk: Keep the removed-hold version low until climbers can downclimb.

items.name: Add-On
items.setup: A bouldering wall and a group of 2 to 6.
steps: The coach adds the first move on an open lane.
Every climber repeats the sequence on their own holds, then the coach adds one move.
A miss means watch the sequence and try again next round. Everyone stays in.
items.why: Memory and route-reading. The sequence grows, and the group tries to beat its own longest chain.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: the team suggests the next move and the coach adds it. Pointer version: a partner on the ground points to the next hold. Lucky Draw: pick a move type from a hat. Board and Dyno versions for teens; Limit Add-On for Ages 14+ (competitive) power days, still one climber on the sequence at a time.
items.risk: Keep sequences on low holds for young groups; teens on boards end before form breaks down.

items.name: Climber Dice
items.setup: Two blank six-sided dice with a different climbing move on each face (heel hook, flag, dyno, toe hook…).
steps: Climbers stand by a bouldering wall and roll both dice.
Climb a problem, or make up a sequence, that uses both moves rolled.
items.why: Random calls make kids review moves they'd usually avoid.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: one die with simpler moves (match, high step).
items.risk: Low wall.

items.name: Climbing Bingo
items.setup: Bingo cards with hold types, moves or routes.
steps: Kids climb to use or find each item on their own card.
Mark the square when done.
The goal is to finish the card, not to finish before someone else.
items.why: Turns vocabulary into a scavenger goal across the session.
items.variations: Pictures for Ages 4–6; techniques and grades for Ages 12+ (training).
items.risk: Spread kids across walls to avoid crowding.

items.name: Scavenger Hunt
items.setup: A list of challenges around the gym (climb an easy problem, do 10 push-ups, climb a route with slopers).
steps: Each climber works through their own checklist, or the class shares one list.
Check an item when it is done. The aim is to finish the list.
items.why: Practice and review: kids explore the gym and use what they have learned.
items.variations: Picture lists for younger kids.
items.risk: Walking only in the gym; stay out of other climbers' fall zones.

items.name: Climb the Rainbow
items.setup: Routes or problems of several colors.
steps: Climb one route of each color in rainbow order.
Check off each color when done.
items.why: Builds volume and gets kids trying new colors and styles.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: any holds of the color. Ages 9–12: a grade limit per color.
items.risk: Climbers wait for a clear wall before starting.

items.name: Country Flag Game
items.setup: Flag cards; each color stands for a route color.
steps: Pick a flag.
Climb one route of each color in that flag.
items.why: Chance-based picking keeps it fun and spreads kids across walls.
items.variations: Skittles version: grab a few candies and climb their colors.
items.risk: Check allergies before using candy.

items.name: Finish Together
items.setup: Small groups of 2–4. Each group has a list of climbs everyone can do.
steps: Each small group works through its list, one climber at a time on a climb.
The goal is for every climber to finish their climbs.
Note how many the group finished and try to raise that number next time.
items.why: Teamwork and planning who climbs what, with lots of volume and a shared goal.
items.variations: Older kids: a fall means lower and restart that climb.
items.risk: Moving on never skips partner checks; boulderers check the fall zone before starting.

items.name: Send Tally
items.setup: Bouldering area and a list of grades.
steps: Climbers have a set time to try problems, one person on a problem at a time.
Each send goes on your own tally, or on a shared team total.
Celebrate the total. Do not rank climbers.
items.why: Teaches choosing climbs wisely and pacing a session, with a shared total and no ranking.
items.variations: The group sets a send total and tries to beat it next session.
items.risk: Remind climbers to check the fall zone before starting.

items.name: Trivia Traverse
items.setup: Trivia cards; a traverse wall.
steps: Ask a trivia question; a right answer earns the next move along the wall.
Each climber finishes the traverse at their own pace.
A miss means another try on the next turn.
items.why: Mixes vocabulary review with climbing.
items.variations: Climbing vocabulary questions.
items.risk: Low traverse.

items.name: Match
items.setup: Bouldering room; players take turns.
steps: Someone on the ground picks a hold.
The climber gets on and finds a way to match it: both hands, or a heel hook, toe hook or knee bar.
Count your own solid matches and try to beat that count.
items.why: Creative problem-solving on one hold: heel hooks, toe hooks and hand matches.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: big holds and hand matches only.
items.risk: Climb down rather than drop from awkward positions.

items.name: Beat the Clock
items.setup: A timer and a traverse wall.
steps: Each climber starts with hands and feet on.
On go, get as far across as you can in 10 seconds; stop on “time”.
Mark your own distance and try to pass it. Add time in later rounds.
items.why: Fluid movement with a short personal goal.
items.variations: Harder: repeat the exact same holds. On top rope, climb as high as you can in 10 seconds and note your own high hold.
items.risk: Low traverse; on Time's Up the belayer keeps pace with fast climbers.

items.name: Dyno Count
items.setup: Bouldering wall with plenty of jugs.
steps: Start matched on a jug and dyno to a hold of your choice.
Dyno again, without coming off, and count your own links.
Rest, then try to beat your own count.
items.why: Practises dynamic movement and power against your own mark.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): short sideways dynos. Ages 14+ (competitive): bigger, vertical ones.
items.risk: Spotter ready; clear mat; limit attempts to protect shoulders.

items.name: Dyno Dash
items.setup: Two holds a reachable jump apart.
steps: Dyno from one hold to the other.
Increase the gap only when you stick the current one.
Mark your own best distance and try to pass it.
items.why: Explosive power and accuracy, measured against your own best distance.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): short sideways dynos. Ages 14+ (competitive): bigger, vertical ones, still against your own mark.
items.risk: Land on feet on a clear mat; spotter in place.

items.name: Flying Squirrel
items.setup: A low start and a distant jug over a clear mat.
steps: The climber launches toward the jug.
Catch it or not, they land the same way: feet, then bottom, then roll onto the back.
items.why: Commitment to dynos plus repeated falling practice.
items.variations: Lower start for younger kids.
items.risk: Low start only, one at a time; run Learn to Fall first.

items.name: 1-2-3 and Jump
items.setup: A low wall or volume.
steps: Count 1, 2, 3 with arm swings, then jump to a target hold.
Run-and-jump version: a short run into a jump.
items.why: Rhythmic counting helps time dynamic moves.
items.variations: Bigger targets for younger climbers.
items.risk: Clear mat and spotter; low targets.

items.name: King Swing
items.setup: A top rope from an anchor two stations over, about 10–15 feet to the side of the route being climbed.
steps: Climb an approachable route on that offset rope.
Let go and enjoy a big pendulum swing on the rope.
items.why: Hailey Caissie runs it for birthdays: a thrilling way to build trust in the rope.
items.variations: Lower starting height for first-timers.
items.risk: Coach-run only: clear the whole swing arc of people and features, and use an experienced belayer.

items.name: Volume Stay
items.setup: A large volume on a low wall.
steps: Each climber gets one attempt at a time to reach the top of a big volume.
Time how long you can stay on it with quiet feet.
Rest, then try to beat your own time.
items.why: Balance, body tension and grip strength, measured against your own stay.
items.variations: Note the time and try again after a rest.
items.risk: One climber at a time; clear mat below.

items.name: Flash or Fail
items.setup: Routes or problems nobody in the group has tried.
steps: Pick a climb you've never attempted.
Try to flash it; if you fall, you can't try again until everyone else has had a go.
items.why: Builds onsight reading, commitment and a tolerance for falling short.
items.variations: Add a read-out-loud step before each attempt.
items.risk: Problems well within ability so one try doesn't push form.

items.name: Silent Shapes
items.setup: Teams of 3–4, one per coach; a designated route or wall.
steps: One climber at a time goes up and holds a pose for a shape (square, star, animal).
The group guesses the shape.
Swap climbers. There is no winning team.
items.why: Balance and endurance: holding a pose means finding good holds and body position.
items.variations: Younger kids: simple shapes on a low boulder.
items.risk: On top rope or low; the climber lowers or steps down when tired.

items.name: Paper Fortune Teller
items.setup: Paper fortune tellers with climbing moves inside.
steps: Pick a color and number.
Do the move revealed inside.
items.why: Random picking keeps practice varied and fun.
items.variations: Kids design their own fortune tellers.
items.risk: Low wall.

items.name: Under Pressure
items.setup: Four boulders with 5+ moves, one or two grades below each climber's max flash; a stopwatch.
steps: Each climber sets a time limit, rest included, to finish all four.
Round 1: climb all four, resting when needed, and record your own time.
Rest, then try to beat your own time in round 2.
items.why: Physical and mental endurance. A personal challenge against your own clock.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): three boulders and a looser limit.
items.risk: Rest is part of the plan; stop if form breaks down.

items.name: Golf
items.setup: Several routes well within everyone's ability; each is a hole.
steps: Climb the route and count every handhold you use.
A fall adds three to your own count.
Rest, then try to lower your own count.
items.why: Rewards reading the sequence and moving with intent, countd against your own count.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: count holds only, no fall penalty.
items.risk: Skipping holds means bigger moves: easy terrain, spotters or top rope.

items.name: Wimbledon
items.setup: A slab or corner climb; a tennis ball in each hand.
steps: Climb the route holding the balls.
You may pinch jugs with your fingertips, but try not to press the balls onto the wall.
Rely on balance and footwork.
items.why: Forces using feet and body position instead of grip.
items.variations: One ball for younger kids.
items.risk: Easy terrain or top rope.

items.name: Balloon Traverse
items.setup: A balloon and a traverse.
steps: One at a time, traverse with quiet feet and straight arms while bouncing a balloon along the wall.
Finish the traverse without dropping it.
Try again to make your own feet quieter.
items.why: Freeing a hand for the balloon forces straight arms and quiet, precise feet.
items.variations: A bigger balloon for younger kids.
items.risk: Check for latex allergies; low traverse.

items.name: Fartlek
items.setup: A long traverse or auto-belay.
steps: Climb continuously, mixing slow and fast sections.
Coach calls changes.
items.why: Varying intensity trains endurance and recovery on the wall.
items.variations: Shorter sets for Ages 12+ (training).
items.risk: Stop if form breaks down.

items.name: Quickdraw Carry
items.setup: Two traverses, each with a bolt at the start and the end; 4–5 quickdraws clipped at each bolt.
steps: One climber at a time traverses to a draw, clips it on their harness, and traverses to the finish.
The group moves every draw.
A drop means rest and try that carry again.
items.why: Endurance and one-handed balance, plus practice handling gear, with one climber on the wall.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): clip the draw onto the finish bolt correctly.
items.risk: Low traverse; no passing on one wall without a plan; check any dropped draw.

items.name: Beat Your Own Laps
items.setup: 1–2 problems well below the group's max flash grade; a timer; groups of 5–6.
steps: Set an order so only one climber is on the problem.
For 5 minutes, take turns climbing it smoothly and hopping off at the top. Count your own clean laps.
Rest 2 minutes. The group adds the laps and tries to beat its own total on the next problem.
items.why: Smooth laps on easy problems. Count your own clean laps, then try to beat that count.
items.variations: Count the group's total laps and try to beat it.
items.risk: The next climber starts only after the last has landed and cleared the mat; downclimb when possible.

items.name: Silent Feet
items.setup: An easy traverse or route.
steps: Look at the foothold before you place your foot.
Place it without making any noise.
If a foot thuds or scrapes, redo that placement.
items.why: Silence is only possible when eyes guide the foot and the weight moves smoothly, so it trains precise, controlled feet; it's the most common footwork drill in climbing coaching.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: sneaky ninja or mouse feet. Ages 6–9: Jingle Feet (bells on shoes; keep them quiet). Ages 12+ (training) and Ages 14+ (competitive): silent feet on harder warm-up circuits.
items.risk: Low traverse or top rope; everyone else quiet so the climber can hear.

items.name: Sticky Feet
items.setup: An easy traverse or route.
steps: Pick the best spot on each foothold, like a bull's-eye.
Place the foot there and don't adjust or move it once it's down.
Speed up as accuracy improves.
items.why: No readjusting forces careful first placements, so feet become accurate and trustworthy.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: glue feet story. Ages 9–12: count readjustments and try for zero. Ages 14+ (competitive): on small holds.
items.risk: Low or roped terrain.

items.name: Bean Bag Feet
items.setup: Two bean bags per climber; a traverse.
steps: Place a bean bag on top of each shoe.
Traverse as far as you can without losing them.
Mark how far each climber gets.
items.why: Feet that slap or swing drop the bags, so kids learn to place feet gently.
items.variations: Mark how far you got, then try to pass your own mark.
items.risk: Low traverse.

items.name: Foot Notes
items.setup: Coins or bean bags placed on footholds along a traverse.
steps: Use any handholds but only the footholds with an object on them.
Place your foot on the free part of the hold without knocking the object off.
items.why: Forces careful looking and exact placement.
items.variations: Look Out for Choss!: bean bags as the ‘choss’ for intermediate climbers.
items.risk: Low traverse; collect fallen items before the next climber.

items.name: Foot Stab
items.setup: Stand on the ground, about a leg's length from the wall.
steps: Balance on one leg.
With the other foot, reach out and touch a hold accurately and with control.
Choose trickier targets to increase difficulty.
items.why: Off-the-wall accuracy and balance practice before climbing.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: big colorful holds as targets.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Foot Placement Focus
items.setup: A traverse or route.
steps: The coach picks a part of the foot or a specific foot to climb with.
Climb with only the left foot, only the toes, only the heels, and so on.
items.why: Exploring each part of the foot shows climbers how many ways a foot can be used.
items.variations: Younger: one rule per climb.
items.risk: Easy terrain.

items.name: Connect the Dots
items.setup: Chalk dots (tick marks) on wall features or footholds.
steps: Use any handholds.
Feet only on the chalk dots.
items.why: Targets on blank wall teach smearing and trust in friction.
items.variations: Fewer dots for older climbers.
items.risk: Low terrain.

items.name: Toe Touches
items.setup: Easy boulders.
steps: Start the problem as normal.
Lightly tap the next handhold with a foot before moving the hands.
items.why: Opens the hips and builds balance and high-step mobility.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: tap only low holds.
items.risk: Easy problems only.

items.name: High/Low Feet
items.setup: A traverse or route.
steps: Climb with feet as close to the hands as possible.
Then climb on tiptoes with hands and feet stretched as far as possible.
items.why: Feeling both extremes helps climbers find the efficient middle.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: alternate every three moves.
items.risk: Low traverse.

items.name: Step Step Reach
items.setup: A traverse or roped climb.
steps: Move the feet two or three times before each hand move.
Say it out loud: step, step, reach.
items.why: Builds the habit of climbing with the legs first.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: chant it together. Older: step, step, reach on vertical and slab.
items.risk: Easy terrain.

items.name: Drag a Hold
items.setup: Small and medium handholds on the floor within reach of the climber's feet.
steps: The climber stays on the wall, facing mostly in.
Use only the feet to drag a hold to a target spot.
Count your own successful drags and try to beat that count.
items.why: Toeing in and pulling with the foot builds steep-wall foot strength and control.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): smaller holds. Ages 14+ (competitive): steeper wall.
items.risk: Stay low; clear the dragged holds from the landing zone after.

items.name: Heel Tugs
items.setup: Vertical wall (easier) or overhang (harder).
steps: Find a foot position where you feel you're toeing in.
Pull back with the heels, as if dragging the hold toward you, then relax.
Repeat on different footholds.
items.why: Teaches active toeing in, which keeps feet on steep walls.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): on vertical. Ages 14+ (competitive): on overhang.
items.risk: Low holds.

items.name: Small Feet
items.setup: A section of wall; mark small footholds if sizes vary.
steps: Traverse using only small footholds.
Trust Your Feet version: only tiny screw-ons, divots, waves in handholds, sloping holds and wall features.
items.why: Builds trust in poor feet and precise placement.
items.variations: Progress to routes with small feet.
items.risk: Low or roped terrain.

items.name: Sticky Foot Throws
items.setup: Two jugs to hang from where the feet won't touch the ground.
steps: Hang with feet cut.
Raise one foot at a time to a set hold to the left or right.
Stick it and keep it there without it slipping.
items.why: Advanced steep-terrain footwork: landing feet precisely after cutting.
items.variations: Closer holds to start.
items.risk: Short sets; land on feet on a clear mat.

items.name: Smearing Drill
items.setup: A jug at a comfortable height.
steps: Hang from the jug.
Walk your feet up as high as possible, then back down, without footholds.
items.why: Feeling friction on blank wall builds trust in smears.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: smear while a coach spots.
items.risk: Low jug; step off to the mat.

items.name: Single Leg Smear
items.setup: A route climbed twice.
steps: First climb: smear only with your right foot; the other foot uses footholds.
Second climb: smear only with your left.
items.why: Balances smearing skill on both sides.
items.variations: On slab for beginners.
items.risk: Top rope or low boulder.

items.name: No Hands Slab
items.setup: A slab or dihedral (corner) wall.
steps: Climb using no handholds, or only one hand.
Use opposition in a corner if needed.
items.why: Makes the legs and balance do the work.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: one hand only.
items.risk: Low slab or top rope; step down when stuck.

items.name: Foot Switching
items.setup: Two handholds and one foothold.
steps: Switch feet on the foothold 10 times in a row without falling off.
Stay as controlled as possible.
Try different sizes and types of footholds.
items.why: Teaches the hop and slide switches needed on small holds.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: a big foothold.
items.risk: Low holds.

items.name: Quick Step
items.setup: As in 10 Seconds.
steps: Play 10 Seconds.
While one person counts, another calls frontstep, backstep, instep, or a combination.
Climbers change foot positions on each call.
items.why: Fast practice of the three foot positions.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: one call at a time.
items.risk: Low holds.

items.name: Downclimbing
items.setup: A vertical or slab route on top rope, or any boulder.
steps: Climb up the route.
Climb back down instead of being lowered (or jumping).
The belayer gives enough slack that the climber is never hanging on the rope.
items.why: Looking down at footholds builds eye-to-foot contact; downclimbing boulders is the best way to reduce landing impacts.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: downclimb the last two holds. Ages 9–12: whole route. Ages 14+ (competitive): downclimb warm-up laps.
items.risk: Belayer keeps the rope just snug, not tight; boulderers downclimb to a low height, then step off.

items.name: Climber Up–Climber Down
items.setup: Groups of 2 or 3; a route or problem.
steps: One climbs while the others call “climber up” or “climber down”.
The climber follows the calls, moving up or down.
items.why: Builds downclimbing and endurance, and keeps the group engaged.
items.variations: On top rope with a belayer who keeps up.
items.risk: Belayer manages slack carefully during direction changes.

items.name: Disco Climbing
items.setup: A top-rope or lead route.
steps: Climb to the first bolt, then downclimb.
Rest at the bottom if needed.
Climb to the second bolt, downclimb, and repeat until the top.
items.why: Builds endurance and downclimbing confidence.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: up to the third bolt only.
items.risk: On top rope for anyone not yet lead-certified; belayer keeps up with slack.

items.name: Skipping Holds
items.setup: A climb around 5.7–5.9/10a, climbed twice.
steps: First time: use every foothold.
After lowering, climb again skipping at least one foothold each time.
items.why: Forces high steps and rock-overs.
items.variations: Skip handholds too for Ages 14+ (competitive).
items.risk: Top rope.

items.name: Robot Arms
items.setup: A short instructional wall, or only halfway up a route; ‘robot arm’ braces (or cardboard tubes).
steps: Put a robot arm on each arm after tying in.
Climb keeping arms straight and using the legs to move up.
items.why: Straight arms let the skeleton hold weight, saving muscle.
items.variations: No props: monkey arms, hang long like a monkey.
items.risk: Keep it low so arms aren't locked from too high.

items.name: Hang or Hold
items.setup: One or two holds per climber.
steps: Hang with bent arms for as long as you can (or a set time).
Rest.
Hang with straight arms and compare.
items.why: Kids feel how much easier straight arms are.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: big jugs and short counts.
items.risk: Feet stay near the mat; low holds.

items.name: Tap Your Thumbs
items.setup: An easy route or traverse.
steps: On every hold, tap your thumb three times while still holding on.
items.why: Brings awareness to over-gripping and loosens the grip.
items.variations: Coach calls ‘tap’ at random holds.
items.risk: Easy terrain.

items.name: Hover Hands
items.setup: A moderate or easy route.
steps: Lock off with one hand.
Hover the other hand over the next hold for three seconds before grabbing it.
The belayer and coach can count out loud.
items.why: Builds controlled, static movement and lock-off strength.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: hover for one second. Ages 14+ (competitive): hover on steeper terrain.
items.risk: Top rope or low; stop when form breaks.

items.name: Keep the Tension
items.setup: Two handholds and two footholds fairly close together; a 20–30 second goal.
steps: Keep your feet on the same holds.
Move your hands up the wall one or two holds at a time and back down while holding body tension.
items.why: Teaches holding the feet on through core and body tension.
items.variations: Ages 14+ (competitive): on overhangs.
items.risk: Low holds.

items.name: Reposition Repetition
items.setup: All climbers on the wall with two hand and two foot holds.
steps: Call a limb to remove (right hand, left foot).
Keep the body and trunk in balance without that limb.
Replace and call another.
items.why: Teaches climbers to shift weight to stay in balance.
items.variations: Faster calls for older climbers.
items.risk: Low holds.

items.name: Triangles
items.setup: Easy routes or problems.
steps: Climb making a triangle with your body: hands up high, feet wide.
Check the triangle at each stance before the next move.
items.why: A simple, fundamental balance builder kids can picture.
items.variations: Draw the triangle on a whiteboard first; Ages 9–12: notice when an upside-down triangle (hands wide, feet together) works better.
items.risk: Low holds.

items.name: One Arm, One Foot
items.setup: A traverse or sequence.
steps: Try to complete it using one arm, or one foot.
items.why: Builds deadpointing, body tension, strength and balance.
items.variations: On a route, boulder or traverse.
items.risk: Low terrain; step down when stuck.

items.name: Weak Hand Climb
items.setup: A moderately challenging route or problem.
steps: Use your non-dominant hand for all the crucial holds.
items.why: Builds ambidexterity and body awareness.
items.variations: Hand behind back for teens.
items.risk: Easy terrain or top rope.

items.name: Peter Pans
items.setup: An overhanging route.
steps: Cut feet on every move.
Control the swing before the next move.
items.why: Teaches control of dynamic movement and builds grip.
items.variations: Keep it to a few moves; save it for mature teens.
items.risk: For older teens only (about 16+); limit reps to protect growing fingers and shoulders.

items.name: Dead Hang
items.setup: A big jug or bar.
steps: Hang with active shoulders (pulled down, not shrugged).
Brief holds, rest, repeat.
items.why: Builds grip endurance and shoulder engagement.
items.variations: Feet on a box to reduce load.
items.risk: Teens only, jugs only, brief holds; no small edges or fingerboards for growing climbers.

items.name: Pivot Practice
items.setup: Two footholds and two handholds.
steps: Reach as high as you can with one arm without moving anything else.
Then stay on the holds and pivot the feet (turn in or out) and reach again.
items.why: Shows how turning the hips adds reach.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: big holds.
items.risk: Low holds.

items.name: Clockwork
items.setup: A large multi-directional hold (or a cluster of holds facing different ways).
steps: Move through several hand and body positions on the one hold before going to the finish.
Hold Recycler: set a problem that forces using one hold several ways.
items.why: Practises reading hold direction and moving the body to match it.
items.variations: On a spray wall for Ages 14+ (competitive).
items.risk: Low hold.

items.name: Balanced Flag
items.setup: A tape mark, balance pod or marker on the ground for each climber.
steps: Stand on one foot and flag the other out to the side.
Time your own hold.
Switch feet, then try to beat your own last time.
items.why: Off-the-wall introduction to how a flag balances the body, measured against your own last hold.
items.variations: Eyes closed for older kids.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Flag Boxes
items.setup: Colored tape on each shoe (right red, left blue) and matching tape on footholds.
steps: Climb a problem where each foot may only use holds of its color.
Flag when your foot has no hold.
items.why: Forces flagging decisions.
items.variations: Fewer taped holds for Ages 14+ (competitive).
items.risk: Low problems.

items.name: Step Flag Reach
items.setup: An easy route with plenty of holds.
steps: Follow the pattern step, flag, reach all the way up.
items.why: Repetition makes flagging automatic.
items.variations: Inside and outside flags.
items.risk: Top rope or low.

items.name: Monkey Tails
items.setup: An easy boulder or top-rope route.
steps: Climb the whole route with only one foot.
Use the other foot as a monkey tail, swinging it to keep balance.
items.why: Kids feel how a flag counterbalances.
items.variations: Switch feet next lap.
items.risk: Easy terrain.

items.name: Team Reach Challenge
items.setup: Groups of two or three of similar height; set start hand and foot holds.
steps: Start on the holds and reach as far as you can using a flag.
Mark your own farthest hold.
Rest, then try to pass your own mark.
items.why: Shows how far a good flag extends reach. Note your own mark and try to pass it.
items.variations: Try both directions and keep the better of your own two marks.
items.risk: Low holds.

items.name: Heel and Toe
items.setup: An area with large holds.
steps: Use a heel or toe hook for 5–6 moves in a row.
Or traverse using only heel and toe hooks.
items.why: Builds confidence in hooks, which feel strange at first.
items.variations: Bat hangs with a close spot and a toy to pick up underneath.
items.risk: Bat hangs only with a coach spotting closely, low, over a clear mat.

items.name: Static and Dynamic
items.setup: A route 5.9 or easier, or 3–4 boulders.
steps: Climb it twice back to back.
First as statically as possible (lock off and hover).
Then as dynamically as possible.
items.why: Contrasts the two styles so climbers can choose.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: slow sloth and quick frog.
items.risk: Rest 2 minutes between problems.

items.name: Setter for a Day
items.setup: A quiet or kids-only area; tape.
steps: Each kid (or pair) sets a problem with a set number of moves.
Others try it.
Tape the Movement: coaches pre-tape holds to force high steps, rock-overs or flags.
items.why: Setting teaches how holds force movement.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: four-move problems.
items.risk: Low problems only.

items.name: Any Feet One Color Hands
items.setup: Problems with taped handholds.
steps: Hands only on one color.
Feet on anything.
Progress to feet-follow-hands.
items.why: A stepping stone to following a full route.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: big holds.
items.risk: Low problems.

items.name: Systems Wall Drills
items.setup: A systems wall; three climbers, one per color.
steps: Choose one hold type (pinches, slopers).
Two 20-second sets bumping hands, 10 seconds rest.
Speed version: matching holds, feet fixed.
items.why: Structured hold-type and movement practice.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): bumping only.
items.risk: Teens only, short sets, stop when form breaks.

items.name: Read and Point
items.setup: A route or problem the climber hasn't tried.
steps: Before touching the wall, point to each hand and foot hold in order and say the moves.
Climb it.
Afterwards, say what matched your plan and what changed.
items.why: Reading first saves energy and builds the onsight skill used in competitions.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: point to the next three holds only. Ages 14+ (competitive): visualize with eyes closed and time the read like a comp observation period.
items.risk: Read from outside the fall zone of other climbers.

items.name: Draw the Route
items.setup: Paper and pencils; a boulder or route.
steps: Give kids a set time to read a climb (shorter for experienced climbers).
They turn around and draw it from memory.
Compare drawings to the wall, then climb.
items.why: Sequence reading and memory; prepares climbers for comp observation.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: draw only the hand holds.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Guess the Grade
items.setup: An unfamiliar section of wall; sticky notes over the grade tags.
steps: Each kid guesses the grade after reading and/or climbing.
Reveal the grade and talk about what you noticed. There is no ranking.
items.why: Builds reading and stops grades from deciding whether kids try a climb.
items.variations: No Tag, No Problem: pick climbs from too far back to see grades.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Opposite Day
items.setup: An easy boulder; two colors of tape.
steps: Kids identify which holds are for the right hand and which for the left.
Mark them with two tape colors.
Climb it using right-hand holds with the left hand and vice versa.
items.why: Reading hand sequences and solving a familiar problem in a new way.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: three or four holds.
items.risk: Easy boulder.

items.name: Wrong Beta Only
items.setup: A climb with an obvious sequence.
steps: A coach or climber shows the intended beta.
Climbers find a completely different way to do it.
items.why: Easiest isn't the goal: exploring new movement grows the toolbox.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): change only one section.
items.risk: Stay on terrain well within ability.

items.name: The Beta
items.setup: A boulder problem; a coach on the wall.
steps: Climbers coach the coach through the problem with words.
The coach does exactly what they say, funny mistakes included.
items.why: Kids learn to read routes, communicate and think through problems together.
items.variations: Kids must use climbing vocabulary.
items.risk: Low problem; the coach chooses when to step off.

items.name: Beta Swap
items.setup: Pairs on the same project.
steps: Each climber tries the problem their own way.
Explain your beta to your partner.
Try your partner's beta and pick the best parts of each.
items.why: Height and style change the best beta; sharing builds problem-solving and respect.
items.variations: Ages 14+ (competitive): film both and compare.
items.risk: Partners spot each other.

items.name: Observe Others Climbing
items.setup: A route or problem you just climbed.
steps: Watch an advanced climber on the same climb.
Note how they move, which footholds they use, and why.
Or watch World Cup videos for footwork details.
items.why: Watching skilled climbers gives a model to copy.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): write one footwork detail to try.
items.risk: Watch from outside fall zones.

items.name: Video Self-Review
items.setup: A phone on a stand (with permission per gym and family rules).
steps: Film an attempt.
Watch it once for feet, once for hips, once for breathing.
Pick one change for the next attempt.
items.why: Teens can see what they can't feel.
items.variations: Side-by-side with a partner's beta.
items.risk: Follow gym filming and privacy rules; family consent for minors.

items.name: Best and Worst Holds
items.setup: A list of hold types: directionals (undercling, sidepull, gaston), crimp, pinch, sloper.
steps: Each kid chooses a favorite and least favorite.
Share out loud if time allows.
Climb at least one route or 2–3 boulders featuring each.
items.why: Kids name and practise weaknesses, not just strengths.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: pictures of holds.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Marked Routes
items.setup: Bright paper tags on the route cards of climbs chosen for the class.
steps: Kids climb only tagged routes that day.
Remove all tags after class.
items.why: Steers kids onto chosen hold or wall types and keeps them in the right area.
items.variations: Tag by theme: all slopers this week.
items.risk: Tags keep kids on climbs coaches have checked.

items.name: I Went to the Wall…
items.setup: A bouldering wall with varied holds.
steps: The coach says “I went to the wall and found a…” plus 1–4 hold types.
Everyone finds and uses those holds properly.
Move around between calls.
items.why: Builds hold recognition and correct use.
items.variations: Mini progression: one hold type at a time for younger kids.
items.risk: Spread climbers across the wall.

items.name: Find That Hold
items.setup: One rope as a guide line and one container with one of every hold type. Blindfolds optional.
steps: One person at a time is blindfolded, or closes their eyes.
Call a hold type. They crawl along the rope, feel for it, and bring it back.
The group is done when every hold type has been found.
items.why: Teaches hold types by touch, with one shared goal for the class.
items.variations: No blindfold for younger kids: eyes closed.
items.risk: Crawl only; clear floor.

items.name: Blindfolded Hold ID
items.setup: A bucket of holds; a blindfold.
steps: A blindfolded kid picks a hold from the bucket (or is led to the wall).
Feel it and name the type.
Switch.
items.why: Climbing is tactile; knowing holds by feel is the first step to using them.
items.variations: Rock Game: get to know a rock, pass them behind backs and find yours by touch.
items.risk: Belay-line game: stay out of the belayer's space.

items.name: Wall Types
items.setup: Groups of 2 or 3; a sheet of wall types.
steps: Each kid climbs one route on every wall type (slab, vertical, overhang, arete, corner).
The class checks off a wall type when someone has climbed it.
items.why: Kids feel how wall angle changes technique.
items.variations: Edit the sheet to fit ability.
items.risk: Roped walls with a checked belayer.

items.name: Learn the Grades
items.setup: A stack of route cards.
steps: The group puts the cards in order from easiest to hardest.
They work together until the order is right.
items.why: Kids learn how the YDS and V scales work.
items.variations: Pair new climbers with experienced ones.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: ABCs of Climbing
items.setup: Groups of 3–6; one A–Z worksheet and a pencil each.
steps: Set an 8–10 minute timer.
Fill in a climbing word for each letter.
See how many you can fill, then try to beat your own list next time.
items.why: Fast vocabulary review.
items.variations: Ages 4–6 and Ages 6–9: coach writes, kids say.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Traffic Jam
items.setup: A tarp with a grid; a coach knows a secret path.
steps: Players line up beside the grid and step in one at a time, silently.
Paths go sideways or forward only.
A wrong square gets “Traffic Jam!” and the team starts over.
items.why: Teamwork and memory without talking.
items.variations: Shorter paths for younger kids.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Belly Breathing
items.setup: Seated, then on an easy wall.
steps: Sit, close eyes, breathe so the belly grows and shrinks.
Then on the wall: a belly breath each move while sinking the weight lower.
Talk about how it felt.
items.why: Calm breathing relaxes the grip and helps with nerves.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3): balloon belly. Ages 12+ (training): count 4 in, 4 out at rests. Ages 14+ (competitive): compare breathing on onsight and redpoint grades.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Pace Yourself
items.setup: Different routes; a belayer with a timer.
steps: Climb at slower and faster paces on different terrain.
Time each and notice what feels natural.
items.why: Steep or hard climbs need you to move faster through cruxes.
items.variations: Pair with Fartlek.
items.risk: Stop when form breaks.

items.name: Tennis Ball Focus
items.setup: 1–2 tennis balls per climber; open wall space.
steps: On the wall, throw a ball against the wall and catch it one-handed.
Progress to two balls, overhand and underhand.
items.why: Hand-eye coordination and balance while focused on something else.
items.variations: If catching is hard, bounce it off the ground instead.
items.risk: Low holds; nobody behind the thrower.

items.name: Pre-Climb Routine
items.setup: Any climb.
steps: Check (partner check or fall zone).
Breathe twice.
Read the first moves.
Say a cue word, then go.
items.why: A repeatable routine lowers nerves and builds consistency, especially at comps.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: three steps. Ages 14+ (competitive): individual routines.
items.risk: The check comes first, every time.

items.name: Goal Setting & Training Log
items.setup: Notebooks or a shared log.
steps: Write one goal at the start of the month.
Each session, log what you climbed and one thing you learned.
Review monthly.
items.why: Tracking effort and learning supports a mastery mindset.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: sticker chart. Ages 14+ (competitive): training block notes.
items.risk: Log pain or soreness too, and tell a coach.

items.name: Smooth Repeat
items.setup: A climb the climber has already sent.
steps: Climb it again more smoothly: fewer readjustments, quieter feet.
Rate smoothness 1–5 and try to improve.
items.why: Repeating a known climb lets kids focus on quality.
items.variations: Partner rates smoothness.
items.risk: Easy terrain.

items.name: Choose-Your-Level Ladder
items.setup: Three or four problems of rising difficulty for each climber.
steps: Climbers pick where to start.
Move up a rung after a send, down after two falls.
items.why: Lets each child work at the right challenge (mastery, not ranking).
items.variations: Celebrate personal bests.
items.risk: Fall zones clear between rungs.

items.name: Climbing Science
items.setup: Whiteboard or a demo on low holds.
steps: Explain one idea: friction, center of gravity, levers, or how a belay device adds friction.
Demonstrate it.
Climbers test it on the wall.
items.why: Understanding why a technique works helps older kids use it.
items.variations: Pick a weekly topic.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Teach-Back
items.setup: Pairs or small groups.
steps: One climber teaches a skill to another (with a coach listening).
Swap.
items.why: Teaching is the best test of understanding.
items.variations: Ages 14+ (competitive) teaches a skill to a younger group with a coach present.
items.risk: Coaches verify anything involving ropes or systems.

items.name: Team Send Board
items.setup: A whiteboard tally.
steps: Set a group goal (total sends or vertical feet).
Each send goes on the board.
Celebrate when the group hits it.
items.why: A shared goal builds team culture and volume.
items.variations: Monthly team goals.
items.risk: Quality over quantity; stop when form breaks.

items.name: Precision Speed
items.setup: An easy, known route.
steps: Climb it fast but with perfect foot placements.
Any readjustment means slow down next lap.
items.why: Keeps precision when moving quickly.
items.variations: Partner calls readjustments.
items.risk: Easy terrain.

items.name: Redpoint Tactics
items.setup: A project route.
steps: Break it into sections.
Work moves, then link sections.
Plan rests and clips; go for the redpoint.
items.why: Teaches the process of working a hard climb.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training) on boulders.
items.risk: Rest between attempts; watch fingers.

items.name: Limit Bouldering
items.setup: Hard boulders near the climber's max; long rests.
steps: Few attempts per problem.
Rest 3–5 minutes between tries.
Stop when quality drops.
items.why: Short, high-quality efforts build power.
items.variations: Pair with Limit Add-On (see Add-On).
items.risk: Older teens only; limit volume; watch fingers and shoulders.

items.name: 4x4s
items.setup: Four boulders well within ability (ideally ones you've done).
steps: Climb each problem 4 times in a row with little rest.
After all four, rest 4 minutes.
Repeat for 4 sets.
items.why: Classic power-endurance circuit.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): 3x3 or easier problems.
items.risk: Problems well below max; stop if form breaks down.

items.name: Two in a Row
items.setup: An onsight-grade route; belay pairs.
steps: Climb, lower, climb again with little rest.
Switch with your belay partner.
items.why: More climbing time and endurance.
items.variations: Downclimb instead of lowering.
items.risk: Partner check each time you re-tie or re-clip.

items.name: Climb Your Age
items.setup: Pairs of similar age; the whole class period.
steps: Each climbs as many pitches as they are years old.
Downclimbing can count as a pitch; 2x2s help.
Rules: no repeats, mixed styles.
items.why: Endurance and energy management over many climbs.
items.variations: Older kids: half their age.
items.risk: Rest between pitches whenever you need it; belay checks every climb.

items.name: Climbing Pyramid
items.setup: A pyramid template for each kid.
steps: Onsight grades on the bottom, project at the top, one grade in between.
Climb six climbs: start bottom left, go up, then down the right side.
items.why: Structured volume and a clear plan.
items.variations: Bigger pyramid for Ages 14+ (competitive).
items.risk: End on easy climbs.

items.name: Easy Continuous Laps
items.setup: An easy traverse or auto-belay.
steps: Climb easy terrain continuously for several minutes.
Shake out on good holds.
items.why: Low-intensity volume builds aerobic endurance.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): 3–5 minutes. Ages 14+ (competitive): longer.
items.risk: Very easy terrain only.

items.name: Power Endurance Circuits
items.setup: A circuit of moderate moves (20–30).
steps: Climb the circuit, rest equal time, repeat.
items.why: Trains the pump of a hard route.
items.variations: Fewer moves for Ages 12+ (training).
items.risk: Older teens only; stop when form breaks.

items.name: Harness Check
items.setup: Harnesses laid out on the mat.
steps: Step in: leg loops not twisted, waist above the hips, buckles doubled back or locked.
Freeze for a coach check and name each part you checked.
Accuracy is the goal. Try again until the check is complete.
items.why: Makes the harness routine automatic. A complete check matters more than speed.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: coach helps, kid names each part. Ages 12+ (training): check a partner's harness too.
items.risk: A coach checks every harness before anyone leaves the ground.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays (if using for auto belay)

items.name: Partner Check
items.setup: Belay pairs, tied in and ready.
steps: Check each other: harness buckles, figure-8 finished and through both tie-in points, belay device and locked carabiner on the belay loop, rope end knotted.
Say it out loud and point at each item.
items.why: A spoken, pointed check is the habit that catches mistakes.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: coach-led check song. Ages 14+ (competitive): lead-specific additions.
items.risk: No check, no climb, every time.

items.name: Knot Practice
items.setup: Spare ropes on the belay line.
steps: Teach or review a knot.
Kids help teach each other.
Each climber ties it until it is complete and dressed, then checks a partner's knot.
items.why: Keeps waiting climbers engaged while building an essential roped-climbing skill.
items.variations: Teach new knots to interested climbers.
items.risk: Practice knots never replace a coach check on a real tie-in.

items.name: Spot the Figure 8
items.setup: Pre-tied knots, some correct and some not (or photos).
steps: Kids sort correct and incorrect figure-8s.
Explain what's wrong in each.
items.why: Recognizing a correct knot is the first step to checking one.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: count the five pairs of strands.
items.risk: Practice ropes only.

items.name: Flake and Coil
items.setup: Spare rope sections.
steps: Show how to flake a rope and why, and how to coil it.
Each climber practises until the rope feeds without a tangle.
items.why: Rope handling for future lead and outdoor climbing.
items.variations: One climber practises while a partner watches the pile.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: What Is Wrong?
items.setup: A quiet top-rope wall; coaches set up with deliberate mistakes.
steps: Coaches prepare to climb with things done wrong: leg loops upside down, shoes too big, chalk bag like a purse, laces undone, device on the tie-in loop instead of the belay loop, decorative carabiners.
The class finds what's wrong and what risk each mistake creates.
items.why: Kids learn to spot problems before a climb starts.
items.variations: Kids set up mistakes for each other (coach-supervised).
items.risk: Mistakes are shown on the ground only; nobody climbs on them.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays (when demo includes auto belay)

items.name: Climbing Commands Call-and-Response
items.setup: Group on the mat.
steps: Coach calls a command; kids answer: “On belay?” – “Belay on.” “Climbing.” – “Climb on.” “Take.” – “Got you.” “Lower.” – “Lowering.”
Mix up the order; whoever answers wrong leads the next round.
items.why: Clear, standard commands manage risk on every climb.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: “Ready?” – “Ready!” Ages 14+ (competitive): add lead calls like “slack” and “clipping”.
items.risk: Always use the gym's standard commands.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays

items.name: Ground School Belay
items.setup: A rope through a low anchor or a coach holding the climber end; a backup belayer.
steps: Practise the belay motion (pull, brake, under, slide) with a coach.
Hold the brake strand at all times.
Progress to a backed-up belay on the wall.
items.why: Builds the brake-hand habit before any real weight.
items.variations: Ages per gym policy; teens follow belay test steps.
items.risk: Backup belayer and coach supervision until certified.

items.name: Astronaut Lowering
items.setup: A top-rope route.
steps: At the top, sit back like in a chair with feet flat on the wall.
Walk down like an astronaut while being lowered.
items.why: Teaches the lowering position and builds trust in the rope.
items.variations: Start from a low height for nervous kids.
items.risk: Belayer lowers slowly; feet stay out in front.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays (auto-belay version)

items.name: Top-Rope Fall Practice
items.setup: A top-rope route with an attentive belayer.
steps: Climb a little way, call “falling”, and let go.
Increase height and slack slowly.
Climber chooses when to progress.
items.why: Gradual exposure builds trust in the rope.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: “sit in the chair” version.
items.risk: Belayer keeps the rope snug; check the fall line is clear.

items.name: Lead Fall Progression
items.setup: Steep, clean terrain; a qualified lead belayer and coach.
steps: Start with falls at the clip, then slightly above.
Progress gradually as the climber chooses.
Practise falling posture: look at the wall, legs bent, arms off the rope.
items.why: Lead falls are a skill to practise with care, not avoid.
items.variations: Only after the climber is lead-certified.
items.risk: Steep, clear terrain; experienced lead belayer; coach present.

items.name: Ground Clipping Practice
items.setup: Quickdraws on a low bolt or board.
steps: Practise clipping with both hands.
Check rope direction to avoid back-clipping.
Avoid z-clipping by grabbing rope close to the knot.
items.why: Correct clipping is automatic before it's used up high.
items.variations: Timed clipping drills.
items.risk: On the ground only until certified.

items.name: Mock Lead
items.setup: Top rope plus a second rope trailing to clip.
steps: Climb on top rope while clipping a second rope into draws.
Coach checks clips.
items.why: Practises lead skills with a top-rope backup.
items.variations: Add timed clips.
items.risk: Top rope is the real belay; the lead rope is for practice only.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays (if auto-belay backup)
Top-rope backup or auto-belay backup checked

items.name: Spotting Practice
items.setup: A low boulder.
steps: Spotter stands with soft hands near the climber's hips.
Guide the fall toward the mat; don't catch.
items.why: Spotting directs falls to manage risk on boulders.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3): parent spotting hands.
items.risk: Spot only low problems.

items.name: Fall Zones Tour
items.setup: Walk the gym.
steps: Point out fall zones under each wall.
Practise walking around, not under, climbers.
Teach three golden rules: look up, stay off mats under climbers, listen to coaches.
items.why: Kids learn where risk is in the gym.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: ‘wiggle zone’ and ‘fall zone’.
items.risk: Ongoing coach supervision.

items.name: Cool-Down Stretch & Reflect
items.setup: Mats in a circle.
steps: Gentle stretches for forearms, shoulders and hips.
Each kid shares one thing they got better at.
End with a team cheer.
items.why: Calm finish, reflection supports a growth mindset.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3): parent and child stretch together.
items.risk: Gentle stretches only.

items.name: Story Stretch
items.setup: Mats.
steps: Tell a short story where each part is a stretch (tall tree, sleepy cat, frog).
Kids act it out.
items.why: Keeps young kids engaged while cooling down.
items.variations: Kids add a part to the story.
items.risk: Gentle stretches only.

items.name: Pass the Animal
items.setup: A soft toy, and a shelf, bucket or big jug as a hand-off spot at the edge of each wall panel; one climber per panel on a low traverse.
steps: The first climber carries the toy across their panel and leaves it on the hand-off spot.
They step down; then the next climber climbs to the spot, picks up the toy and carries it across their own panel.
Count the team's hand-offs in one round and try to beat that count next round.
items.why: Climbing one-handed while carrying the toy teaches balance, and the team count motivates without ranking.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: pass while on top rope next to each other.
items.risk: One climber per panel, and nobody climbs toward, above or below another climber.

items.name: Beat Your Own Time
items.setup: 1–2 problems or a short list of routes well below each climber's max flash grade; a stopwatch per climber or pair.
steps: Each climber picks their climbs and an order; one climber on a climb at a time.
Time your own lap from first touch to a controlled finish, topping or downclimbing.
