Rest, then try to beat your own time while keeping feet quiet and placements clean.
Write your best in your log. Times are never compared between climbers.
items.why: Smooth, efficient movement under a clock, measured only against your own best. Planning your own list also builds pacing.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: one easy boulder and two tries. Ages 12+ (training): a short circuit of 3–4 routes. Ages 14+ (competitive): count your own clean laps in 5 minutes and beat last week's count.
items.risk: The next climber starts only after the last has landed and cleared the mat; moving on never skips partner checks; stop if form breaks down.

items.name: Welcome to the Wall
items.setup: Floor spots or tape marks on the mat about 8 inches from a low traverse; 3–4 spots per panel.
steps: Kids line up at one end of the wall.
Everyone walks slowly along the wall in one direction, hands on handholds and feet only on the floor spots.
Feel the holds and pick the ones you'd use if you were climbing; keep an arm's length apart.
After two or three passes, talk about which holds felt best and why.
items.why: Everlast uses it as a first-day, no-climbing introduction: kids touch holds and practise hand-foot coordination with zero height, which lowers first-day nerves.
items.variations: Parent & Child 2–3: walk it holding the parent's hand. Ages 3–4: name each hold's color as you touch it. Ages 6–9: on the last pass, lift one foot onto the lowest foothold for a breath.
items.risk: One direction of travel only, arm's length spacing, and nobody walks under another climber's fall zone.

items.name: Target Practice
items.setup: Beanbags or soft objects placed on holds along a low traverse; hoops or tape shapes on the mat as targets.
steps: One climber per panel; the next starts when the one ahead reaches the second panel.
On each panel, take one object off a hold and toss it into a target on the floor.
Reach the end, climb down, step off the mats and rejoin the line.
Count the group's total hits and try to beat it next round.
items.why: Letting go with one hand to throw trains one-handed balance and weight over the feet; a group total keeps it about personal and team bests.
items.variations: Ages 3–4: big targets right below the wall. Ages 6–9: objects on very high or very low holds. Ages 9–12: targets farther away or smaller. Seasonal themes: pumpkins into harvest hoops, or bean bags into jack-o'-lantern targets.
items.risk: Use only soft targets on the mats (hoops, tape), never hard buckets under the fall line; throwers wait until the mat in front is clear.

items.name: Catch-n-Climb
items.setup: One soft ball per wall panel; a tosser standing at the edge of the mat in front of each panel; a tally sheet.
steps: Climbers traverse with one climber per panel and a steady line waiting.
When a climber is level with a tosser, they stop, turn, catch the ball one-handed and toss it back.
Climbers and tossers count successful catches and add them to the group sheet.
Swap tossers and climbers so everyone does both.
items.why: Catching while on the wall forces a stable stance and good weight on the feet; Everlast frames it as a whole-group goal of most total catches.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: underhand tosses from close. Ages 9–12: different ball sizes. Ages 12+: set a group catch target before starting and try to beat it.
items.risk: Soft balls only; tossers stay at the edge of the mats, never under a climber; keep one climber per panel.

items.name: Spell It Out
items.setup: Letter cards placed on holds along a traverse.
steps: Give the group a word.
One at a time, each climber traverses and collects the next letter in the word; one letter per climber.
Climbers on the floor help find where the next letter is.
Lay the letters out in order on the floor until the word is spelled.
items.why: Every climber's turn moves the team toward one shared result, and searching for a letter makes kids scan and move across the whole wall.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: their own name or a three-letter word. Ages 6–9: climbing words (SMEAR, CRIMP). Ages 9–12: letters on harder holds or higher.
items.risk: One climber on the traverse at a time per section; the spotting line stays outside the fall zone.

items.name: Number Pairs
items.setup: Cards numbered 1–10 placed on holds along a traverse.
steps: Pair climbers up and give each pair a target total (for example 9).
Each partner traverses and collects one card so the pair's two cards add up to the target.
Pairs plan which numbers to fetch before getting on the wall.
Return the cards and give the next pair a new total.
items.why: Partners have to plan and communicate before climbing, and the collected cards give a clear finish without ranking anyone.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: totals under 10. Ages 9–12: subtraction or multiplication, bigger numbers, or three cards per pair.
items.risk: One climber per section; partners wait off the mats.

items.name: Beta Map
items.setup: Part 1: a 4x4 grid of loose holds or spots on the floor. Part 2: a spray wall or traverse area. The coach secretly maps a start-to-finish sequence.
steps: The first climber stands on the start and moves to any neighboring spot; the coach says yes or no.
A right move means go again; a wrong move ends the turn and the next climber starts from the start, repeating the revealed sequence before guessing the next move.
Keep going until the whole sequence is found and every climber can move through it.
Repeat the same rules on the wall with a sequence every climber can do, starting with open feet.
items.why: Climbing Wall Association example game for planning, remembering and executing beta; the whole team succeeds together when the sequence is solved.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: floor version only, short sequence. Ages 9–12: on the wall with open feet. Ages 12+: feet on or off in the sequence.
items.risk: Wall sequence well below everyone's limit and low; waiting climbers stand off the mats.

items.name: Same Hand, Same Foot
items.setup: A vertical wall with lots of jugs.
steps: Place the right foot, then move the right hand.
Place the left foot, then move the left hand.
Keep arms long while moving the feet and shifting weight; bend them only to move up.
items.why: Momentum calls it the most basic movement pattern in climbing and recommends teaching it in a climber's first days, before route reading or flagging.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: say it out loud as they climb. Ages 9–12: add open and closed hip positions. Ages 12+: point out the exceptions (back flag, pogo).
items.risk: Easy, low terrain; stop and reset if arms bend and the climber locks up.

items.name: Hip Rotation Drill
items.setup: An easy boulder.
steps: Climb it once turning the opposite hip to the wall (reach left hand, right hip in).
Climb it again turning the same-side hip to the wall (reach left hand, left hip in).
Talk about which felt more balanced and how much farther you could reach.
items.why: PitchSix uses the awkward first lap to make the same-side hip rotation rule obvious: better balance, less grip effort and more reach.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: big holds and a partner who calls which hip. Ages 12+: on steeper terrain. Ages 14+: combine with flagging.
items.risk: Well below limit; downclimb or step off when a position feels awkward.

items.name: Slow-Motion Climbing
items.setup: 6–8 boulders 2–3 grades below flash, including some the climber usually rushes.
steps: Climb each boulder as slowly and smoothly as possible: no jumping or swinging.
Set feet and hips before every reach; the move is continuous, not stop-start.
Rest a minute or two between boulders.
Move up a grade only when all of them stay slow and clean.
items.why: Blok Sessions: taking momentum away shows every sloppy foot placement and builds body tension and control.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: vertical walls with good feet, or slow only the feet. Ages 12+: add steeper terrain. Ages 14+: same boulders, slower.
items.risk: Steep slow moves load shoulders and core; stay on vertical terrain if a shoulder is sore and stop when movement gets scrappy.

items.name: Antagonist Push Set
items.setup: Floor space; light resistance bands or very light weights for shoulder rotations.
steps: Two sets of push-ups.
Two sets of dips (assisted if needed).
One set each of external and internal shoulder rotations.
Use loads light enough for about 20 reps; 15–20 minutes, two or three times a week.
items.why: Climbing trains pulling muscles; Eric Hörst and UKC's junior injury interviews recommend balancing them with push and rotator-cuff work to lower elbow and shoulder injury risk.
items.variations: Ages 12+: push-ups and band rotations only. Ages 14+: full set; add reverse wrist curls.
items.risk: Light loads and clean reps only; nothing to failure; no finger loading added.

items.name: Plumb Line
items.setup: A low traverse on a vertical wall. Tie a figure 8 (or a small carabiner) on a short cord and hang it from the climber's waist so it swings freely in front of the hips.
steps: Start the traverse with the line hanging in front of the hips.
A foot may only move when the plumb line hangs directly over the other foot.
Pause, shift the hips until the line settles over the standing foot, then move the free foot.
Traverse back the other way.
items.why: The line makes center of gravity visible: climbers see whether their weight is really over the standing foot before the next foot moves, which is the heart of weight transfer.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: a beanbag on a string and a 'hips over the foot!' call. Ages 9–12: hands may only move while the line is still. Ages 12+: try a slightly steeper wall and notice how the hips have to come in.
items.risk: Keep the cord short so it cannot loop around a foot or a hold; low traverse only, never on a rope route.

items.name: Circle Circle
items.setup: A circle about 1–1.5 m across marked with chalk or tape on a low wall section with plenty of holds (or a hoop fixed flat to the wall).
steps: The climber starts on the wall at the edge of the circle.
For one minute, climb around the circle and count complete laps.
Rest, then try to beat your own lap count.
Switch direction each round.
items.why: Going round a circle mixes up, down and sideways moves without stepping off, so climbers practice changing direction, crossing and matching; counting your own laps is a personal-best goal.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: a big circle, any holds, count out loud together. Ages 6–9: climb inside the circle only. Ages 9–12: hands outside the circle, feet inside.
items.risk: A hoop must not be able to catch a foot (chalk or tape avoids that). Keep the circle low so every lap stays within jump-down height over mats.

items.name: Hidden Rest
items.setup: A traverse or easy route with a few spots where a one-hand or no-hands rest is possible (a big foot ledge, a corner, a volume).
steps: Demonstrate a few rest positions: weight over a big foothold, stemming in a corner, hips against a volume.
Climbers search the section for 'hidden rests' and show one to the group.
At each rest they let go with one hand (then both, if possible) and shake out.
Climb the section again, using every rest they found.
items.why: Finding a stable position over a good base of support takes weight off the arms; climbers who spot rests climb longer before getting pumped.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: 'can you find a spot where you can wave both hands?' Ages 9–12: rate each rest good, okay or poor. Ages 12+ and 14+: plan rests from the ground, then check the plan on the route.
items.risk: Demonstrate first and give precise instructions; no-hands rests only low on the boulder wall or on top rope.

items.name: The Artist
items.setup: A sheet of paper with an outline of a face fixed to the wall at a reachable height, and a marker.
steps: Each climber climbs to the picture and adds one feature (an eye, a nose, a hat).
They draw with one hand while holding on with the other and both feet on holds.
Climb down; the next climber adds the next feature.
Finish the picture as a team and show it off.
items.why: Drawing frees one hand, so climbers must find a stable base of support first; the shared picture keeps everyone involved without ranking anyone.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: picture low, on big holds. Ages 6–9: reach the picture by a given route. Ages 9–12: the group names the next feature before each climber starts.
items.risk: Keep the picture within jump-down height on the bouldering wall and spot one-handed attempts; cap the marker between turns.

items.name: Posing
items.setup: A slab or vertical wall with lots of holds; the group sits on the mat.
steps: One climber gets on the wall and finds a funny or spectacular position (a star, a flag, a frog).
They hold it for three seconds while the group claps or cheers.
The group gives the pose a name.
The next climber tries a pose nobody has done yet.
items.why: Kids discover positions they would never try on a route, building coordination, body awareness and flexibility; the cheer celebrates creativity, not a ranking.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: coach calls a theme (animals). Ages 9–12: each pose must use a named technique (drop knee, flag). Ages 12+: link three poses into a short sequence.
items.risk: Start new climbers on a slab before vertical; keep poses low and step down from awkward positions instead of letting go.

items.name: Rope Corridor
items.setup: Two ropes or cords stretched horizontally along a traverse, about knee height and shoulder height, forming a corridor.
steps: Traverse with both hands and both feet inside the corridor.
If a hand or foot lands outside, pause and fix it before moving on.
Traverse back.
items.why: A narrow band of usable holds forces small, precise moves and creative footwork.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: a wide corridor. Ages 9–12: narrow it. Ages 12+: hands above the top rope line, feet inside the corridor.
items.risk: Fix the cords flat to the wall so nothing can snag a foot or finger; low traverse only.

items.name: Split the Line
items.setup: A rope or tape line running from bottom to top of a low wall section.
steps: Climb up with both hands on one side of the line and both feet on the other.
Climb down, then switch sides and go again.
items.why: Splitting hands and feet across a line forces climbers to lean, twist and flag to stay in balance.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: big holds near the line. Ages 9–12: shift the line so one side has few holds. Ages 12+: on a steeper panel.
items.risk: Low terrain over mats; tape the line flat so nothing swings into the climber.

items.name: Climb to the Beat
items.setup: A speaker and a playlist mixing slow and fast songs; an easy traverse.
steps: Play a slow song: climbers move slowly and smoothly with the tempo.
Switch to a fast song: move faster while keeping feet quiet.
Change songs without warning; climbers match the new tempo.
items.why: Matching movement to tempo trains pace control and smooth flow, contrasting slow precise movement with quick light movement.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: one move per drumbeat, counted out loud. Ages 9–12: one move per bar. Ages 12+: slow tempo on easy sections, brisk tempo through the hard part.
items.risk: Low traverse with climbers spread apart; keep the volume low enough to hear the coach.

items.name: Hip Watch Traverse
items.setup: A quickdraw clipped to the harness or a bright sticker at the climber's hip; an easy traverse with big footholds.
steps: Traverse sideways while keeping your eyes on the marker at your hip.
Notice how the hip turns in and out as you move.
Traverse again normally, keeping that hip close to the wall.
items.why: Watching the hip makes climbers aware of hip position and turning, which drives reach and balance on traverses.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: a sticker on the hip. Ages 9–12: turn the hip to the wall on each reach. Ages 12+: pair it with the Hip Rotation Drill.
items.risk: Big footholds and low terrain only, because the climber is not looking at their feet.

items.name: Lemon Lime
items.setup: A boulder problem one or two grades below the climber's max flash grade.
steps: Lemon: from the start holds, make the first move, then reverse back to the start.
Without coming off, make the first two moves and reverse to the start.
Keep adding one move until you reach the finish hold.
Lime: from the top, downclimb one move and climb back up; keep adding moves until you are back at the start.
items.why: Repeating and reversing every move builds endurance, sequence memory and downclimbing control on a single problem.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: lemon only, on a short, easy problem. Ages 9–12: lemon only. Ages 12+: full lemon and lime. Ages 14+: closer to flash grade.
items.risk: Choose problems well below max; stop when form breaks or fingers tire, and downclimb rather than fall from the top.

items.name: Special Number Climb
items.setup: Number cards taped high and low across a traverse wall, some that fit today's category and some that don't.
steps: Announce today's special number category (even, multiples of 5, prime).
Climbers spread out, one per wall panel.
On each panel, touch one card that fits the category and say it out loud.
Repeat the traverse finding different numbers.
items.why: Hunting for the right card makes climbers look around, reach and plan their path, with a classroom link and no ranking.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: even or odd. Ages 9–12: keep a running total of the numbers touched.
items.risk: One climber per panel; keep cards within the matted traverse height.

items.name: Hover Feet
items.setup: An easy traverse or boulder well below the climber's level.
steps: Lift a foot and hold it just above the next foothold for a slow count of two while watching it.
Place it on the best part of the hold and don't adjust it.
Repeat for every foot move; hands move as normal.
items.why: Hovering only works when the weight is balanced over the standing foot, and the pause makes the first placement exact; it builds the eye-to-foot habit.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: hover for a count of one. Ages 14+ (competitive): steeper terrain or smaller footholds.
items.risk: Low traverse or top rope; step down if the standing leg starts to shake.

items.name: Mantle Practice
items.setup: Low ledges, volume tops or boulder top-outs with thick mats underneath.
steps: Get both hands on top of the ledge.
Flip one hand palm-down and press, then bring a foot up, often right beside the hand.
Lean in over the feet and stand up. Do each mantle 3–5 times, both sides.
items.why: Mantles show up on most boulder top-outs, but kids rarely practise them on purpose; it's like climbing out of a pool.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: ‘climb out of the pool’ onto a stack of mats or a low volume. Ages 12+ (training): mantles with few or no footholds.
items.risk: Keep mantles low over thick mats; spot top-outs and keep the landing zone clear.

items.name: Drop-Knee Finder
items.setup: Easy overhanging boulders with big holds and footholds wide of the body.
steps: Try a move with the hips square to the wall.
Try it again, turning the knee on the same side as the reaching hand in and down while both big toes push on the footholds.
Compare the reach and arm effort. Find 4–6 moves where it helps and do each 3 times per side.
items.why: Feeling the with-and-without difference teaches when a drop knee takes weight off the arms.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: one or two big, obvious moves set by the coach. Ages 14+ (competitive): smaller footholds and steeper walls.
items.risk: Drop knees load the knee: keep reps low, skip very deep or wide drop knees, and stop if the knee twinges.

items.name: Barn-Door Fix
items.setup: A low move that makes the climber swing open (barn-door), such as a long reach off a sidepull.
steps: Try the move with an outside flag and notice where the body swings.
Try it again crossing the free leg behind the standing leg (back flag / reverse flag).
Talk through which version stopped the swing and why.
items.why: A back flag (also called a reverse flag) keeps balance through hand moves without moving the feet; comparing the two flags shows when to use it when X-motion is broken.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: coach sets one clear move. Ages 14+ (competitive): climbers find barn-door moves on their own projects.
items.risk: Low problems over mats; an open swing can pull a climber off.

items.name: Place, Shift, Move
items.setup: A vertical or slab wall with tape on a few high footholds out to the side.
steps: Place: put a foot on a taped hold.
Shift: move the hips over that foot until the weight is fully on it.
Move: only then reach for the next hold, standing up with the leg rather than pulling. Do 3 slow tries per side.
items.why: The three-word cue makes the rock-over a repeatable sequence and shows that the legs do the lifting.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: say ‘place, shift, move’ out loud. Ages 12+ (training): higher footholds and smaller handholds.
items.risk: Low wall or top rope.

items.name: Arch Circuit
items.setup: A wall section with two marked ends and a top height; tape or chalk.
steps: Climb up from one end, across at the top height and down the other end, like an arch.
Walk back to the start and climb another arch using different hand holds; tape each hold once it's used.
Count your rounds in a set time (1–5 minutes) and try to beat your own count next session.
items.why: Builds endurance and quick on-wall decisions, because the easy holds get used up.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: one minute and a low arch. Group version: the group shares one arch and sees how many different arches it can find together.
items.risk: One climber on an arch at a time; keep the arch low and the fall zone clear.

items.name: G-Tox Shake-Out
items.setup: A traverse or route with a good jug rest partway.
steps: At the rest, hang on a straight arm and shake the free arm down by your side.
Then alternate: hold the free arm above your head for a few seconds, then drop it below the waist.
Swap hands and notice which method helps you recover.
items.why: In a study reported by Training for Climbing, alternating the arm above the head and below the waist (G-Tox) recovered grip strength better than dangling alone.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: learn to straight-arm and shake first. Ages 14+ (competitive): use it on pumpy circuits.
items.risk: Practise on easy terrain; come down when pumped rather than hanging on.

items.name: Furthest-Point Traverse
items.setup: An easy traverse.
steps: Every new hand or foot placement must land further along than the last placement of any limb.
Plan which limb goes next; you'll need cross-throughs and step-throughs.
Traverse 8–12 moves, rest a minute, then go the other way. If you break the rule, go back one move.
items.why: Forces sequence planning, cross-throughs and hip turns.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: only the hands follow the rule. Ages 14+ (competitive): longer traverses on steeper walls.
items.risk: Low traverse; rest between attempts.

items.name: One Thing at a Time
items.setup: Easy boulders.
steps: Move only one body part at a time: one hand, or one foot, or the hips.
Pause briefly after each movement.
Make it stricter: move the hips as their own step before each reach.
items.why: Shows where balance or sequence is off.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: robot voice and a ‘beep’ between moves. Ages 12+ (training): steeper terrain.
items.risk: Easy, low boulders.

items.name: Tendon Glides
items.setup: No equipment; seated or standing.
steps: Cycle smoothly through five hand shapes: fingers straight, tabletop, straight fist, hook fist, full fist.
Go for 45 seconds, rest 15 seconds; three rounds, both hands at once.
Follow with easy climbing.
items.why: Moves the finger tendons through their full range before they're loaded; it's a warm-up, not a strength exercise.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: name the shapes (flat, table, fist, hook, ball) as a follow-along.
items.risk: Gentle movement only; nothing should hurt.

items.name: Hollow Body Hold
items.setup: Mats.
steps: Lie on your back and press the lower back into the mat.
Lift the shoulders and legs a little off the mat, arms reaching past your head, and hold without the back arching.
Build to 4 holds of about 20 seconds with a minute's rest.
items.why: Bodyweight core tension that carries over to keeping the feet on steep walls; bodyweight exercises suit youth climbers.
items.variations: Easier: bend the knees or bring the arms to the sides, or do dead bugs (lower one arm and the opposite leg slowly while the back stays down).
items.risk: Quality over time; stop when the lower back lifts.

items.name: Comfort-Zone Ladder
items.setup: One move or boulder that feels a little scary but has a clean, well-padded landing: a high top-out, a committing slab move, a dyno.
steps: First try: go only as far as feels fine, then step or downclimb off.
Each next try: one small step further (one hold higher, one more move).
If a try feels more than a little scary, repeat the previous step. Finish on a step you'd gladly do again.
items.why: Small, chosen steps grow confidence without flooding the climber with fear.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: coach and climber agree the steps in advance. Ages 14+ (competitive): pair with a written fear inventory after the session.
items.risk: Only over good landings, with spotting where useful; never practise above a poor landing.

items.name: Backstep Drill
items.setup: 5–6 easy, slightly overhanging boulders with footholds out to the side.
steps: On each reach, put the outside edge of the shoe on the same side as the reaching hand onto a foothold.
Turn that hip into the wall so the body goes sideways, then reach.
Climb each boulder 2–3 times, backstepping wherever it helps, and notice how much further you reach than with your chest square to the wall.
items.why: Blok Sessions calls turning the hip in the biggest reach gain available on steep walls; easy boulders keep the load low while the habit forms.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: coach marks the backstep footholds with tape. Ages 12+ (training): compare with Hip Rotation Drill. Ages 14+ (competitive): move on to drop knees and twist locks, which build on the same hip turn.
items.risk: Keep it on easy, low boulders over good mats; a turned hip can swing open, so practise the move low before trying it higher.

items.name: Deadpoint Practice
items.setup: Easy boulders with 3–4 long reaches (skip holds to lengthen them).
steps: Choose an exact spot on the target hold, not just the hold.
Swing the hips toward it, push with the feet and catch that spot at the moment the body stops rising, with the feet staying on.
Do 5 tries per move with about a minute's rest, then climb 2–3 easy boulders using deadpoints wherever you can.
items.why: A deadpoint lengthens the reach while the feet stay on, so it replaces slow, strained lock-offs at a low cost.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: big target jugs at a short distance. Ages 12+ (training): smaller target holds. Ages 14+ (competitive): deadpoints into sidepulls and on steeper walls.
items.risk: Catching a hold loads fingers and shoulders: use big targets, keep reps low and rest between tries; climbers coming back from a finger or shoulder injury should get cleared first.

items.name: Climb with Flow
items.setup: 4–5 boulders well within everyone's ability.
steps: Climb each boulder 3 times without stopping between holds.
As you reach, let the hips swing toward the side you're reaching to and let that carry you into the next move.
Rest about a minute between climbs; each lap, try to have fewer pauses than your last lap.
items.why: Linking moves with the hips saves energy; Blok Sessions stresses that continuous is not the same as rushed.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: ‘smooth as honey’ on a big-hold traverse. Ages 12+ (training): film a lap to spot the pauses. Ages 14+ (competitive): take it to problems near flash level.
items.risk: Pick climbs well below limit so flowing never turns into rushing; keep the fall zone clear.

items.name: Step-Up Springs
items.setup: 2 easy vertical boulders with plenty of step-ups.
steps: Climb each boulder 5 times, changing where each step-up starts: lap 1 push from the high knee, lap 2 from the low knee (picture it compressing like a spring), lap 3 low knee then high knee.
Lap 4: start the move from the hips, rounding then arching the back to carry the weight across.
Lap 5: use whichever felt best for each move. Rest 30 seconds between laps.
items.why: Starting the same move from different places teaches climbers to step up with the legs rather than pull with the arms.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: the first two laps only. Ages 14+ (competitive): apply the best version on a current project.
items.risk: Stay on the same easy, low boulders; if the arms are doing the work, slow down and restart.

items.name: One Change Per Try
items.setup: A move on a project that keeps stopping the climber.
steps: After a fall, name out loud what stopped you: strength, a foot error, timing or hesitation.
Pick one change for the next try, in this order: the sequence first (hand order, foot order, another hold), then the body (more tension, hips in, commit), and only then small details.
Say the change before each try, rest about 90 seconds, and note what each change did.
items.why: Changing one thing at a time shows what actually helped; the order (Kris Hampton's beta before microbeta, as described by Blok Sessions) stops climbers fiddling with details when the sequence is wrong.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: a partner or coach helps name the reason. Ages 14+ (competitive): keep a written list of reasons and look for patterns over weeks.
items.risk: Rest fully between tries and cap the number of goes on one move to manage finger and shoulder load.

items.name: Today's Process Goal
items.setup: A notebook or sticky note per climber.
steps: Before climbing, write one or two goals fully in your control, not results (for example, take ten breaths and read the sequence before each try).
Climb the session with those goals in mind.
Afterwards, mark each goal as every time, sometimes or not at all, and write one sentence on what got in the way.
items.why: A result depends on the day; a process goal is something you either did or didn't, so the check afterwards is honest.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: one goal, chosen from a short coach list. Ages 14+ (competitive): keep a goal until it happens every time, then replace it.
items.risk: Pick goals that support good habits, such as checking the fall zone, rather than ones that push past fatigue.

items.name: Three Good Choices
items.setup: End of session, on the mats or with notebooks.
steps: Each climber names or writes three specific choices that worked (a beta decision, resting before trying again, choosing an easier climb to warm up).
Add one thing learned, even from a climb that didn't go.
Finish with one concrete action for next time.
items.why: Most climbers remember only the falls; naming specific good decisions helps them notice what they did well, alongside honest reflection.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: one good choice each, said aloud in the circle. Ages 14+ (competitive): write it on the way home while it's fresh.
items.risk: Celebrate good risk choices too, such as backing off a move that felt wrong.

items.name: World's Greatest Stretch
items.setup: Mats with room to lunge.
steps: Start in a push-up position and step the right foot outside the right hand into a deep lunge.
Drop the right elbow toward the floor, then rotate the chest open and reach the right arm to the ceiling, eyes following the hand.
Hold 2–3 seconds, return and step back; 5 reps per side.
items.why: Opens the hips, upper back and hamstrings in one movement, which helps high steps and turning on the wall.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: ‘reach for the sky’ with a shallower lunge. Ages 12+ (training): deeper lunge and fuller rotation as range comes.
items.risk: Turn from the upper back, not the lower back, and never force range.

items.name: Deep Squat Hold
items.setup: Mats; a pole or door frame to hold if needed.
steps: Feet a bit wider than shoulders, toes slightly out.
Sink as low as comfortable with heels down and chest up.
Hold about 45 seconds, stand and relax 15 seconds; repeat up to 5 times.
items.why: Ankles, hips and lower back all at once; getting comfortable low makes high steps easier.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3) to Ages 4–6: squat like a frog and hop up, holding hands with a grown-up. Ages 12+ (training): rock gently side to side once 45 seconds feels easy.
items.risk: Hold something if heels lift or you tip backward; never force a painful range.

items.name: No-Touch Dynos
items.setup: A slightly overhanging wall with big start holds at chest height and jugs as a target above.
steps: Set up with one foot higher than the other, push from the feet and drive the hips toward the target.
Touch the target holds and let go before taking any weight, landing back on the mat with soft knees.
5 jumps per set-up (left foot high, right foot high, feet level), 30 seconds between jumps and 2 minutes between set-ups.
items.why: Never holding the target lets climbers practise the launch many times without the load of catching it on fingers and shoulders.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): short, straight-up targets. Ages 14+ (competitive): diagonal targets or a steeper wall, then progress to Dyno Dash.
items.risk: Every rep ends in a drop: check the mat and clear the landing zone before each jump, land on the feet with soft knees, and keep the start low.

items.name: Blink Feet
items.setup: An easy traverse or a top-rope route well below the climber's level.
steps: Pick a foothold and start moving the foot toward the exact spot you want.
Just before the shoe touches, close your eyes and finish the placement by feel.
Keep the eyes closed until the foot is set and weighted, say whether it feels right, then open your eyes to check.
Pick the next foothold and repeat for every foot move.
items.why: Mike and Mark Anderson's drill, as described in Climbing and Send Edition, teaches climbers to judge a foot placement by feel first and confirm it by sight, which builds trust in the feet and spatial awareness.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: blink only on big footholds near the ground, with a coach beside them. Ages 12+ (training) and Ages 14+ (competitive): use it on small footholds and jibs.
items.risk: Keep it low on a traverse or on a snug top rope; hands stay on good holds and the eyes open again before any hand move.

items.name: Covered-Hold Climb
items.setup: 3–4 easy, low boulders; paper and tape, or cloths, to cover 2–4 key holds in the middle of each.
steps: Study the boulder and plan the whole sequence, feet included.
A coach or partner covers 2–4 key middle holds you planned to use.
Climb from memory, feeling for each covered hold where you expect it.
If you can't find it within a few seconds, look, correct and keep climbing; afterwards say which holds your memory got wrong.
items.why: Blok Sessions calls covering holds the closest thing to a memory test climbing offers: it checks whether the read holds up once you're on the wall.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: cover only one or two big handholds. Ages 14+ (competitive): cover footholds instead of handholds, which most climbers find harder.
items.risk: Never cover the start holds or a hold needed to climb down; use easy, low boulders with a clear landing and look as soon as a hold can't be found.

items.name: Crux Reverse Repeats
items.setup: A boulder with a crux (hardest section) the climber can already do reliably.
steps: Climb through the crux.
Reverse (climb back down) 1–3 moves.
Climb through the crux again and continue to the top. That's one set.
Rest 3 minutes; do 4–5 sets, ending the set as soon as technique gets sloppy.
items.why: Reversing a few moves doubles the time spent in the hardest section without needing another boulder, building power endurance specific to the climb.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): reverse one move on a crux well below their limit. Ages 14+ (competitive): reverse more moves or add a set, not both.
items.risk: Pick a crux they can do every time, keep full 3-minute rests and stop when form breaks down to manage finger and shoulder load.

items.name: Squeeze Boulders
items.setup: 5–6 steep boulders with big holds or volumes set far apart.
steps: Hold yourself on by pushing the hands toward each other, like hugging a barrel.
Keep the feet pressing into the wall and the core tight so the hips stay close.
Give each boulder 3 tries, resting 2 minutes between tries.
items.why: Compression is a squeeze-in strength that finger strength can't replace, and it shows up constantly on modern, volume-heavy setting.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: hug a big volume or arete for a few moves on a low boulder. Ages 14+ (competitive): wider holds, steeper walls and poorer features.
items.risk: Big holds and low starts for younger climbers; squeeze with the arms and core rather than crimping hard, and rest fully between tries.

items.name: Double-Hand Moves
items.setup: Easy vertical or gently overhanging boulders with big holds; for the first step, a spray wall or board with pairs of jugs.
steps: Hip bounce first: feet on, knees bent, hands on two jugs at chest height. Sag the hips away, then drive them in and move both hands together to two jugs above and back, then two below and back. 3 sets of 5 with 3 minutes rest.
Then on easy boulders, pick moves where both hands can let go and grab the next two holds at the same time, driving with the legs.
Start with small double moves; climb 5–6 boulders a few times each, resting between climbs.
items.why: Blok Sessions uses the feet-on hip bounce as a lower-risk way to learn the weightless moment, then double-throughs teach moving both hands at once, which modern setting asks for and which feels strange until practised.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): hip bounce and small doubles on vertical walls only. Ages 14+ (competitive): bigger doubles, poorer target holds, then steeper walls.
items.risk: Legs drive and arms just grab; feet stay on for the hip bounce, target holds stay big, the landing zone is clear, and full rests keep tired reps from teaching sloppy timing.

items.name: Three Ways to One Finish
aka: All Holds to a Chosen Finish
items.setup: A section of bouldering wall with many holds and one clearly reachable finish hold, ideally in a quiet area.
steps: Pick one finish hold.
Build at least three different start-to-finish sequences that all end on it, each using different holds and footwork.
Climb each one, then compare: which used fewer moves, less effort or better rests?
items.why: Building several ways to the same finish shows climbers how much choice a wall offers and breaks the idea of one correct beta.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: a coach helps point to the holds for two short ways to a big finish jug. Ages 14+ (competitive): pick a hard-to-reach finish so options are scarce, then set the three lines for a partner to try.
items.risk: Keep sequences low and away from other climbers' fall zones; climb down rather than drop from the finish.

items.name: Attempt Budget
aka: Perfect Boulders in the Fewest Attempts
items.setup: 3–4 new or barely tried boulders near the climber's flash level; a notebook.
steps: Before starting each boulder, decide how many tries you get (never more than 10) and write it down.
Aim to climb it perfectly: smooth and controlled, not just to the top.
Rest 2–3 minutes between tries and use the rest to plan the next one.
Next session, try to beat your own budget on new boulders.
items.why: A fixed attempt limit makes climbers think between goes instead of hurling themselves at a problem; a scrappy send doesn't count.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: a budget of 5 tries on easier boulders. Ages 14+ (competitive): lower the limit or move to harder boulders.
items.risk: Full rests between tries; the budget is a cap, not a target, so stop early if fingers or skin feel sore.

items.name: Twist-Lock Builder
items.setup: A steep wall with good holds; room to build 3–4 moves on existing holds.
steps: Build 3–4 moves that need a long reach with nothing to jump off.
Stand on the foothold, turn the knee in and the hip into the wall, and hold the pulling arm bent tight to the body.
Turn, settle, then reach far with the other hand. Practise each move 3–5 times per side, resting between tries.
items.why: A twist lock is a drop knee that ends in a lock-off; turning the hip in lets a climber reach much further than square-on and makes long moves look static.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): jugs for the pulling hand, a big foothold and a target almost reachable from a normal position. Ages 14+ (competitive): longer reaches, then poorer holds.
items.risk: Only once drop knees feel natural and the climber can hold a bent-arm lock-off; keep moves low, both sides equal, and stop at any elbow or shoulder pain.

items.name: Wall Angel Hold
items.setup: A flat wall away from the climbing areas.
steps: Back against the wall, feet about 15 cm away, knees slightly bent; tighten the stomach so the lower back is flat on the wall.
Arms to the sides, elbows at shoulder height and bent to 90 degrees, backs of the hands on the wall.
Press the arms firmly into the wall and hold 60 seconds, breathing normally; rest 45 seconds, 3 holds.
items.why: Wakes up the muscles between the shoulder blades that climbing pulls forward, with nothing but a wall.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: 20–30 second holds. Ages 14+ (competitive): press harder, and later add Y-T raises or face pulls.
items.risk: Shoulders stay down, away from the ears; bend the knees more if the lower back lifts, and stop if it pinches rather than works.

items.name: Side Plank
items.setup: Mats.
steps: Lie on one side with the forearm on the floor under the shoulder.
Lift the hips until head, hips and feet make one straight line, and hold.
Switch sides: 30 seconds per side, 3 rounds, 30 seconds rest. Bend the bottom knee to make it easier.
items.why: Trains the side of the trunk that keeps the hips close to the wall when flagging or climbing sideways, which a front plank leaves alone.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: bent-knee version for 10–15 seconds. Ages 12+ (training): straight legs, then lift the top leg or the top arm.
items.risk: Low risk; a clean bent-knee hold beats a sagging straight-leg one, and both sides get equal time.

items.name: Superman Hold
items.setup: Mats.
steps: Lie face down with the arms stretched in front.
Lift the arms, chest and legs a few centimetres off the floor at the same time and hold 2 seconds.
Lower slowly. 10 reps, 3 sets, 1 minute rest.
items.why: Balances all the front-of-body core work and keeps the lower back strong for body tension on the wall.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: ‘fly like a superhero’ for a count of three, a few times. Ages 6–9: one or two sets of 5. Ages 12+ (training): the full 3 sets of 10.
items.risk: Small, slow lifts only; never jerk the head or lower back up high.

items.name: High-Step Stretch on the Wall
items.setup: An easy vertical wall with footholds at several heights, near the ground.
steps: Place one foot on a high foothold you can reach without pain, hips square to the wall.
Breathe for 10–20 seconds, then gently stand up onto it.
Step down and switch legs; 6 per side, moving the foot higher only when it feels comfortable.
items.why: Mobility work in the exact position climbing uses, which also teaches climbers to trust a high foot.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: five slow breaths on a big foothold at knee height. Ages 14+ (competitive): add a wall squat or pigeon pose if range, not balance, is the limit.
items.risk: Stay low with the hands on big holds; never force a painful range.

items.name: Three Strengths
items.setup: Notebooks or cards, at the start or end of a block of sessions.
steps: List three things you're already good at as a climber, as specifically as you can (footwork on slab, reading sequences quickly, staying calm on high moves).
For each, write one climb or session where it showed up.
Add one small thing you'll do to keep each strength sharp while you work on weaknesses.
items.why: Strengths fade if they're never used; naming them with real examples keeps them in the plan and builds confidence.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: say one strength aloud in the circle and a coach adds an example. Ages 14+ (competitive): redo it at the start of each training block and compare lists over the year.
items.risk: Keep it about each climber's own progress, never ranked against teammates.

items.name: Tense and Release
items.setup: Seated or lying on the mats, before a hard attempt or at the end of a session.
steps: Squeeze one muscle group hard for 5–7 seconds, then let it go and notice the difference: legs, core, shoulders, hands, face.
Or do a body scan: notice tension from feet to jaw and let each spot soften.
Finish with slow breaths through the nose: inhale for 4 counts, exhale for 6–8, so the exhale is longer. 3–5 minutes in total.
items.why: Climbers often arrive at a hard attempt already tense; a few minutes of any of these methods changes how they feel, and it gets more effective with practice.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: stiff like a robot, then floppy like a noodle, one body part at a time. Ages 14+ (competitive): a short version at the base of a boulder before a hard try.
items.risk: Low risk; skip squeezing any body part that is sore or injured.

items.name: Every-Minute Boulders
items.setup: One or more 4–6 move problems the climber has already done; a timer.
steps: At the start of each minute, climb one problem.
Rest for whatever is left of that minute.
Keep going for 6 minutes in a row; after a fall, rest and go again at the start of the next minute.
items.why: Short, repeated efforts on a fixed clock train recovery between hard moves in a few minutes.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): 4 minutes on easier problems. Ages 14+ (competitive): note how many of the six went cleanly and try to improve on it next time.
items.risk: Problems well below the climber's limit; stop the set if movement gets sloppy, and climb down or drop only onto a clear mat.

items.name: Pogo Practice
items.setup: Easy, slightly overhanging boulders with big holds, low to the ground; 4–5 moves where the next hold is just too far to pull to statically.
steps: Stand on one foot on a good foothold with both hands on, then swing the other leg back.
Swing that leg forward hard from the hip and start the pull at the same moment the leg comes forward, pushing off the standing foot.
Catch the target hold with the shoulders pulled down and tight.
Do 3–5 tries per move with 1–2 minutes' rest, then switch which leg swings.
items.why: Blok Sessions describes the swinging leg as free power that most climbers never use: timing the pull with the leg swing reaches holds that a static pull can't.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): one move until the timing feels automatic. Ages 14+ (competitive): steeper ground and worse target holds, then spot pogo moves in the beta of current projects.
items.risk: Easy holds low to the ground over clear, thick mats; swing from the hip, not a knee flick; set the shoulders before launching so the swing doesn't carry the climber off the wall; stop when catches get sloppy.

items.name: Freeze the Catch
items.setup: Easy dynamic moves (small jumps or throws) to big holds on a vertical or gently overhanging wall, low over thick mats.
steps: Throw or jump to the target hold and catch it.
Freeze for a full three-second count with the feet quiet and the shoulders engaged.
Downclimb or drop off with soft knees.
Do 3–5 tries on each of 4–5 moves, resting 1–2 minutes between tries; stop if catches get messy.
items.why: Blok Sessions uses the three-second freeze to train the shoulders and core to absorb the swing of a dynamic catch instead of being pulled off by it; the landing is the skill being trained.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: short throws to jugs with the feet staying on. Ages 12+ (training): small jumps. Ages 14+ (competitive): bigger moves and worse target holds, then move a foot during the freeze.
items.risk: Easy moves to big holds only; a coach watches the fall line and clears the landing; count the freeze aloud so it isn't skipped; end the set when catches get messy.

items.name: Heel-Hook Load Repeats
items.setup: 3 moves on a steep wall where a heel hook helps, on comfortable (not sharp) holds the climber can use again and again; done after a full warm-up.
steps: Place the heel on the hold.
Pull with it: bend the knee and squeeze the back of the leg, using that pull to bring the hips up.
Pause for two seconds, then finish the move or reverse it.
Do 3 tries per side on each move with a minute's rest.
items.why: Blok Sessions notes that most climbers place a heel and then pull with their arms anyway; pausing under load teaches the heel to do real work.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): big holds, slightly steep wall. Ages 14+ (competitive): steeper ground and worse holds, then move a hand while the heel holds.
items.risk: Warm up first, because loading the hamstring at an odd angle is a common climbing injury; stop the session at any twinge behind the knee or in the hamstring; low moves over mats.

items.name: Toe-Hook Tension Pause
items.setup: 3–4 low moves on a steep wall or roof edge that use toe hooks (the top of the shoe hooked behind a hold and pulling).
steps: Get into the toe hook position.
Pause for a counted two seconds with the whole body tight.
Move one hand or one foot without letting the feet swing off.
Do each move 3 times per side with a minute's rest.
items.why: Blok Sessions uses the pause to teach what tension actually feels like, which is hard to learn while moving fast; if the arms are burning, the hook isn't pulling.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: one big toe hook on a jug-rail, pausing with both hands on. Ages 12+ (training): worse hooks and bigger moves from the position. Ages 14+ (competitive): two moves while the hook holds.
items.risk: Low moves over clear mats; feet can cut suddenly, so keep the head and body clear of the wall when they do; both sides, short sets.

items.name: Forearm Self-Massage
items.setup: One massage ball (tennis or lacrosse ball) per climber, or the opposite elbow; a bench or the thigh to rest the forearm on.
steps: Rest one forearm palm-up and slowly roll the ball from wrist to elbow with light, comfortable pressure for about a minute.
On a tender spot, hold the pressure and slowly open and close the hand a few times.
Turn the arm over and do the back of the forearm for a minute.
Switch arms.
items.why: Blok Sessions offers it as a calm wind-down that gets climbers paying attention to how their forearms feel; it notes there is no evidence it speeds recovery, so present it as a wind-down, not a treatment.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: pair it with a quiet one-word check-in about how the arms feel. Ages 12+ (training) and Ages 14+ (competitive): add it after hard sessions as part of the cool-down.
items.risk: Light pressure only, never sharp; a spot that hurts while climbing or stays sore for days goes to a parent or physio rather than being rolled harder.

items.name: Plank Clocks
items.setup: Floor space and the lightest resistance band available, looped around both wrists.
steps: Get into a push-up position with the feet wide and one hand under the middle of the chest.
With the other hand, reach against the band to 1 o'clock, back to start, then 3 o'clock, then 5 o'clock, keeping the hips still.
Keep going until the supporting arm starts to shake, then switch hands.
Do 3 sets with a minute's rest, no more than every other day.
items.why: Holding the body on one hand while the other reaches against a band trains the wrist and shoulder to stay steady under load, which Blok Sessions links to mantles, presses and palming moves.
items.variations: Easier: no band, or knees down. Harder: reach a little further toward each clock position, then move up one band.
items.risk: Lightest band first; stop each side at the shake rather than pushing past it; supporting hand stays under the chest.

items.name: High-Step into Dyno
items.setup: 4–5 low moves from a high foothold to a big handhold (set them if needed), on vertical or slightly overhanging wall over thick mats.
steps: Put a foot high and shift the hips over it.
Stand up explosively in one movement and jump or reach dynamically to the target hold.
Start with short, easy versions and catch with control.
Do 3–5 tries per move with 1–2 minutes' rest.
items.why: Blok Sessions calls generating from a high foot one of the most common modern boulder shapes and one of the least practised; the rock-over feeds the jump.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): short moves to jugs. Ages 14+ (competitive): longer moves and worse catches. If the rock-over is the weak part, do Place, Shift, Move for a few weeks first.
items.risk: Short, easy versions first; low moves over clear, thick mats with a coach watching the landing; stop when catches lose control.

items.name: Cam and Knee-Bar Rests
items.setup: Steep terrain with big features (volumes, roof edges, kneebar slots) low to the ground; knee pads if available.
steps: From the ground, find 4–5 spots where a heel-toe cam (heel pressing down, toes pressing up into something above) or a knee bar (lower thigh wedged under a feature, toes pushing on a foothold below) fits.
Get into the position with both hands on.
Let go with one hand and shake that hand loose, then continue the climb.
Do each spot 3 times.
items.why: Blok Sessions treats these as pure technique that costs almost nothing: learning to spot cams and knee bars from the ground gives climbers rests that others miss.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: a slightly steep feature with the feet close to the floor; take one hand off for a second before trying a full shake. Ages 12+ (training): look for them on current projects. Ages 14+ (competitive): set problems that only work with one.
items.risk: Low features over mats; knee pads or long pants to protect the shin on textured volumes; practise the release slowly so the foot doesn't pop unexpectedly.

items.name: Squeeze the Block
items.setup: A wall to stand beside and a yoga block or folded towel per climber.
steps: Stand on one leg next to the wall.
Lift the other knee high and rotate it to the side, like a high step on the wall.
Put the block between the outside of that knee and the elbow on the same side, press them together and lift the knee a little higher.
Hold 20 seconds, keep breathing, then switch legs; 3 holds per leg.
items.why: Blok Sessions uses it for high steps that fall apart at the top of the move: it trains the hip to keep the knee rotated to the side while standing up.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: hold for 10 seconds with one hand on the wall. Ages 12+ (training): take the wall away. Ages 14+ (competitive): 30-second holds.
items.risk: Stand tall rather than tipping the body; stop if the hip pinches; low-risk floor work with space between climbers.

items.name: One-Rule Laps
items.setup: 6–10 easy boulders or an easy circuit; 2–3 minutes of arm, hip and wrist circles first.
steps: Coach names one movement rule for the lap: quiet feet, straight arms whenever possible, hips close to the wall, no readjusting, or steady breathing.
Climbers lap easy boulders keeping only that rule.
Change the rule every few climbs, never mid-lap.
Switch to a new boulder before movement quality drops.
items.why: Blok Sessions keeps one rule per block so attention stays on movement rather than difficulty; easy boulders make the rule the only challenge.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: one rule for the whole block with a cue word. Ages 9–12: rotate rules every few climbs. Ages 12+ (training) and Ages 14+ (competitive): use it as a short end-of-session technique block or rotate the rule between sessions.
items.risk: Easy, low boulders only; keep the mobility part so the climbing starts warm.

items.name: Forearm Flush Laps
items.setup: A traverse or very easy problems on big holds; a timer.
steps: Climb very easy terrain at a relaxed pace for 90 seconds.
Step off and rest 30 seconds with the arms hanging loose.
Repeat 5 times.
Finish less pumped than you started; if the forearms are getting more pumped, the climbing is too hard.
items.why: Blok Sessions uses easy, low-intensity climbing to move blood through forearms after a hard session; it is part of a cool-down, not a replacement for one.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: three bouts on the easiest traverse. Ages 12+ (training) and Ages 14+ (competitive): five bouts after limit or power-endurance work, then stretch.
items.risk: Big holds and effortless movement only; low traverse with feet near the ground; keep traverse traffic flowing in one direction.

items.name: Hoop Haven
items.setup: 1–3 hula hoops, or one soft 3–4 ft rope or jump rope per pair; a low traverse with thick mats; start with two climbers.
steps: Two climbers get on the traverse linked by a shared hoop (one arm of each climber inside the hoop) or by a soft rope looped at the wrist or tucked at the waistband.
They traverse together, matching speed and talking so the link never breaks.
If the link comes free, both climb down and restart from the start.
After a clean finish, try three climbers with two links, then four climbers with three links (never more than four).
items.why: Everlast’s cooperative linked-traverse challenges (hoop or short rope) force climbers to share pace and talk so one shared group finish stays linked the whole way.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: two climbers, big holds, short panel, hoop version. Ages 9–12: silent round after a talking round, or soft-rope link. Ages 12+: three or four climbers; mark the group’s own finish time and try to beat that group mark while still staying linked.
items.risk: Low traverse only; max four climbers; one panel’s worth of space between groups; no pulling partners off holds; unlink immediately if anyone feels yanked; soft rope only—never climbing hardware as a toy link; if anyone feels pulled off balance, both downclimb and reset.

items.name: Front-to-Back Traverse
items.setup: A low, vertical traverse with big holds and clear mats; experienced climbers only.
steps: Start facing the wall and traverse a few moves.
Carefully rotate until you face out, keeping three limbs on the wall as you turn.
Rotate back to face the wall, then repeat the flip pattern to the end of the traverse.
Step down; rest; try again with quieter feet.
items.why: Everlast’s Front to Back Climb asks climbers to rotate facing out and in while traversing, which demands slow hip control and constant awareness of where the body is relative to the wall.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: one flip mid-panel on the easiest traverse. Ages 12+ (training): flip every panel. Ages 14+ (competitive): slightly steeper ground still kept low.
items.risk: Experienced climbers only; low vertical terrain; stop the turn and downclimb if a foot or hand feels insecure mid-rotate.

items.name: Must-Use Holds
items.setup: Gaffer tape; mark one required hold near the start, several in the middle, and one near the end of a traverse or easy problem.
steps: Climbers may use any other holds, but must use every taped “must-use” hold with a hand or foot as they cross.
After a clean lap, add one more must-use hold and go again.
Optional: climbers choose and tape the next required hold for the group.
Keep the line of travel one direction with spacing between climbers.
items.why: Everlast uses must-use holds as a gentle introduction to following a route: some holds are required, but other holds are still allowed so climbers are not stuck on a full closed circuit yet.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: three required holds on big jugs. Ages 9–12: more required holds or higher ones. Ages 12+: required holds that force a flag or high step.
items.risk: Low terrain; tape marks only (do not cover the usable surface of a hold); clear spacing.

items.name: Thin Ice Zones
items.setup: Bungee, string, artificial web or gaffer tape wrapped around holds to mark out-of-bounds zones (border plus interior); leave clear paths over, under, or around.
steps: Traverse without touching any part of a marked zone with hands or feet.
If you touch a zone, climb down, return to the start, and try again.
Climb slower than usual so you can plan the path.
Opposite-day variation: climb using only the marked zones (add more zones first, or allow three free touches).
items.why: Everlast’s On Thin Ice and Avoid the Spider block whole areas of the wall, which forces new paths and body positions without removing holds one at a time.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: one small zone. Ages 6–9: two or three zones. Ages 9–12+: tighter gaps and the opposite-day version. Halloween theme: spider webs and plastic spiders in the zones.
items.risk: Space zones so a clear path always exists; low traverse; one climber per section; nobody climbs over, under or around another climber.

items.name: Mingle Warm-Up
items.setup: Open floor space beside the wall; a short list of warm-up moves (jumping jacks, easy traverse steps in place, arm circles) and 3–4 discussion prompts about today’s goals.
steps: On the coach’s call, everyone starts the warm-up move.
When the coach calls a number, climbers have five seconds to form groups of that size.
Each small group answers one prompt (for example “How will you support a partner today?” or “What is one climbing goal this session?”) or does a short shared move.
Repeat with new numbers and prompts.
items.why: Climbing Wall Association’s sequencing example uses Mingle Warm-Up to prime social and technical goals before the main activity.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: movement prompts only (“make a shape together”). Ages 9–12: mix movement and goal questions. Ages 12+: questions about partner support and personal process goals.
items.risk: Clear floor space; no racing to groups—five seconds is a gathering cue, not a contest; keep bodies off the mats’ fall zones.

items.name: Partner Goal Session
items.setup: Pairs; a set block of bouldering time; easy-to-moderate problems chosen by each climber.
steps: Before climbing, each partner names their own session goal (they do not need to match).
Partners make a simple plan for how the block will let both work on their goals and how they will support each other (spotting, beta only when asked, rest reminders).
Climb the block following the plan.
End with a one-minute share: what helped, what to try next time.
items.why: CWA’s Partner Bouldering core activity builds peer support and intentional practice without comparing climbers to each other.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: one shared sentence goal each. Ages 12+ (training): write goals in a log. Ages 14+ (competitive): include how rest and attempt limits support the goal.
items.risk: Partners stay clear of each other’s fall line while spotting; goals stay personal, never ranked.

items.name: Equipment Metaphor
items.setup: One piece of spare gym gear per climber (harness, quickdraw, chalk bag, shoe, belay device—clean gear only).
steps: Hand each climber a piece of gear.
Give quiet think-time: how does this piece stand for your climbing goal today, or for how you support teammates?
Each climber shares one sentence with the group.
Collect the gear and close the session.
items.why: CWA’s Metaphor Debrief turns ordinary equipment into a reflection prompt so climbers name goals and support in their own words.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: “This chalk bag is how I…“ with a coach sentence stem. Ages 9–12: full one-sentence share. Ages 12+: link the metaphor to next session’s process goal.
items.risk: Use clean spare gear on the floor, not gear someone is about to climb with; seating outside fall zones.

items.name: Build-the-Move Lab
items.setup: A medium-density boulder wall with volumes and jugs, kept well below limit; coach names one pattern at a time.
steps: Coach names one common pattern (examples from CEC: friction stand-up on a slab volume; volume pull-to-press; skate/step-through initiation; jump to a foot stab; dynamic side reach with an opposite toe hook; stand-up to an overhead press).
Each climber builds that pattern on easy holds and repeats it until it feels familiar.
Rotate to the next pattern.
Keep intensity sub-maximal so attention stays on the shape, not the grade.
items.why: Climbing Escalade Canada’s “Build Me the Move” drill builds recognition of competition-common patterns on ordinary walls without needing new sets.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): two patterns per session. Ages 14+ (competitive): full list across a training block; later spot the same patterns on projects.
items.risk: Easy holds low over mats; no skipping-feet bumps up the wall; stop a pattern that needs a hard dyno until a coach spots the landing.

items.name: Rapid-Fire Reads
items.setup: Coach (or partners) marks 3–5 short boulders from easy to one at-or-just-over limit; a timer.
steps: On each boulder the climber has 30 seconds to read and must start the first try by then.
Up to three tries total on that boulder, then move on—even if the first try sent.
If the first try sent, use tries two and three to change or clean one detail.
Include one boulder that may not go, to practise leaving it behind and starting the next fresh.
items.why: CEC’s Rapid Fire Boulders trains fast reading, between-try decisions, and emotional reset without needing a practice round or rankings.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): four easy-to-moderate boulders, no limit boulder. Ages 14+ (competitive): full set including one limit boulder; partners can set for each other.
items.risk: Clear mats and spotters on the harder boulder; keep most boulders well under limit; no comparing sends between climbers.

items.name: Internal Clock
items.setup: A series of boulders; a 5-minute window per boulder; climber cannot see a clock or ask for the time; coach or partner silently notes attempt times.
steps: Coach sets an objective for the boulder (for example two tries early, one try near the end).
Climber works the boulder for what they feel is five minutes, timing attempts by feel.
After the window, compare the felt plan to the noted times.
Repeat on the next boulder, adjusting the internal sense of rest and effort.
items.why: CEC’s Internal Clock drill builds the feel for work/rest timing that strong athletes use when they are not staring at a clock.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): one boulder, coach calls “halfway” once if needed. Ages 14+ (competitive): full series with different attempt plans per boulder.
items.risk: Stop if the climber is too pumped to move well; easy-to-moderate boulders first; note times privately—no leaderboard.

items.name: 1-3-5 Tension Drill
items.setup: Easy-to-moderate boulder or short traverse; coach explains a 1–5 tension scale before starting.
steps: Define the scale: Level 1 = loose and wiggly; Level 3 = lightly stiff but still movable; Level 5 = rigid like a steel pipe; 2 and 4 sit in between.
Pick one move (or a short boulder). Attempt it three times in a row.
Attempt 1: climb at Level 1 tension. Attempt 2: Level 3. Attempt 3: Level 5.
Afterwards, talk about which level actually stuck the move and where tension was wasted.
Repeat on several different moves until climbers start noticing how much tension a move needs.
items.why: PitchSix's 1-3-5 drill builds awareness of tension and relaxation so climbers stop staying max-tense between hard moves.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: Levels 1 and 5 only, with a coach calling the level. Ages 9–12: full 1-3-5 on one move. Ages 12+ and Ages 14+: whole-boulder version, or a partner calling levels mid-climb.
items.risk: Keep intensity below max so the focus stays on feel, not force; step off cleanly if feet cut unexpectedly.

items.name: Tape Pluck Dyno
items.setup: Fold tape sticky-to-sticky so a short tab sticks out from the wall where a dynamic reach would land; soft mats beneath.
steps: From a solid start, dyno or deadpoint and try to pluck the tape off by pinching it between thumb and index finger.
Aim to hit the tape in one accurate catch; do not drag the hand down the wall from above.
Reset the tape and repeat for several focused tries; each climber tracks their own hits and misses.
Progress by moving the tape farther or to a less obvious spot.
items.why: PitchSix's Dynamic Accuracy Drill trains dyno and deadpoint accuracy without loading fingers on a missed pocket or edge.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: short throws to a dangling ribbon or soft target. Ages 12+ and Ages 14+: farther tape, then lateral dynos as well as vertical.
items.risk: Soft targets only; keep dynos controlled and within each climber's current range; no max-power throws for younger groups; clear landing zone.

items.name: X-Motion Laps
items.setup: Vertical or slightly overhanging wall with plenty of footholds; coach demos left-hand to right-foot, then right-hand to left-foot anchors.
steps: Explain X-motion: balance is anchored across the body (left hand to right foot, then right hand to left foot) so the free hand can move with less effort.
Climb an easy lap while naming each half-X out loud before moving the free hand.
If a barn door starts, pause, rebuild the opposite-limb anchor (or a flag), then continue.
Do 2–4 easy laps focusing only on the X pattern, not the grade.
items.why: PitchSix treats X-motion as the default balanced movement pattern for most climbing moves, which cuts unnecessary lunging.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: coach calls “left–right, right–left” on a traverse. Ages 9–12: silent X-laps. Ages 12+ and Ages 14+: a partner watches for same-side climbing and names it.
items.risk: Stay on easy terrain so balance practice is not mixed with max difficulty; keep space between climbers on a traverse.

items.name: Follow Hands
items.setup: Easy-to-moderate route or traverse with usable handholds that can later become footholds.
steps: Rule: feet may only use holds that a hand has already used on this climb.
Climb up, letting feet track the path hands already took; expect more flags, backsteps and high steps.
If stuck, downclimb or step off and try a different sequence that still obeys the rule.
items.why: Send Edition's Follow Hands drill builds awareness of where feet go relative to hands and trains efficient use of limited holds.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: short boulder with big holds. Ages 12+: before moving a hand, place a foot on that same hold and weight it first. Ages 14+: true hand-foot match leverage before the hand leaves.
items.risk: Choose terrain where high steps fit the group's height; spot overhanging versions; step down rather than drop from awkward matches.

items.name: Rooting Drill
items.setup: Route or traverse with sideways movement; climbers already comfortable with basic flagging.
steps: Instead of only flagging into space, place a foot on a hold toward which the hips need to travel.
Dig into that foot and pull the hips toward it using glutes, hamstrings and lower back—not just the arms.
Repeat on several moves, noticing when a rooted foot replaces a vague smear or flag.
items.why: Send Edition's Rooting drill teaches active feet that pull the body into position, not just passive balance flags.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: one or two obvious sideways moves set by the coach. Ages 12+: alternate Flag Everything laps with Rooting laps on the same sequence. Ages 14+: apply rooting on a current project.
items.risk: Start on a moderate angle; aggressive pulling on polished footholds can slip—reset and choose better rubber contact.

items.name: How Low Can You Go
items.setup: Traverse wall; optional tape line marking a low zone (feet and/or hips below a height).
steps: Challenge each climber to traverse while staying as low as possible without touching the ground.
Personal-best framing: can you stay lower than your last try?
Afterwards, talk about which holds and body shapes made staying low easier.
items.why: Everlast's How Low Can You Go breaks the habit of always climbing high and creates new movement puzzles on familiar walls.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: stay below a tape line at chest height. Ages 6–9: add must-touch-low-holds. Ages 9–12: reverse direction or combine with Silent Feet.
items.risk: Keep feet in the allowed climbing zone of the wall; wait for clear space—nobody dives under another climber.

items.name: Tennis Ball Transfer
items.setup: Traverse panels; a tennis ball starting on the first panel (optionally on a dish hold); a target spot or hold at the far end.
steps: Carry the tennis ball from the start panel to the end panel while staying on the wall.
Hold the ball in one hand, or park it briefly on intermediate dish holds if available.
If the ball drops or the climber touches the floor, restart. Personal completion—not compared between climbers.
items.why: Carrying a ball forces planning, careful feet and climbing with limited hand use.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: short panel, park-and-move version. Ages 9–12: full traverse. Ages 12+: non-dominant-hand carry only.
items.risk: Light ball only; avoid overgripping with the free hand on tiny crimps; choose jug-friendly terrain for younger groups; one climber per section.

items.name: Mystery Moves
items.setup: One 4-foot panel per partnership; two small soft tokens (beanbags); command cards such as “move the blue token to a low red hold.”
steps: Place both tokens on different holds on the panel.
One partner climbs on that panel only; the other draws or reads a command to relocate a token to a new hold (color, height or type).
If the token is already on a matching hold, find a different matching hold. If unreachable, draw a new command.
After about 10 successful moves, partners switch roles.
items.why: Everlast's token-command game mixes listening, precise reaches and creative body positions without ranking climbers against each other.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: coach calls simple color moves for the whole wall. Ages 6–9: partner cards. Ages 9–12: add height and hold-type commands.
items.risk: Keep climbers on their own panel—nobody climbs over others; soft tokens only; cards stay off the fall line.

items.name: Laser Hold Guide
items.setup: Top-rope route that is slightly reachy for the climber; belayer plus a second adult or coach with a laser pointer (never shine near eyes).
steps: Climber starts a defined route. When a move is too reachy, the guide briefly points to an allowed add-on hold from another color or route.
Climber uses only pointed add-ons—not free choice of every hold—so the route structure stays intact.
Optional reverse: start on a dense easy route and have the guide leave holds out with the laser to gradually increase difficulty (personal progression).
items.why: UKClimbing's Ari Schneider tip helps shorter climbers experience higher-grade movement patterns without abandoning route structure.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: coach points with a finger from the ground on a low boulder. Ages 9–12: laser on top rope. Ages 12+: older climbers take turns as pointer for a peer with adult oversight.
items.risk: Never aim lasers at faces or eyes; belay remains primary; add-ons should be realistic—the pointer must be ready to try any move they prescribe.

items.name: Dynamic Movement Warm-Up
items.setup: Open floor space away from fall zones; about 8–10 minutes; no long static holds before climbing.
steps: On-the-wall shapes on the floor (5 reps, hold the end position 1–3 seconds): Sideways Flag, Reverse Flag, High Step, Frogger hip circles, Drop Knee, Rose Move.
Rotations: arms, hips, knees—both directions, 5 each.
Arms: Sun Salute, Cross-Body Swing, Back Taps—5 each.
Wrists and fingers: wrist tendon glides and finger tendon glides—10 each.
Then easy climbing as a pulse raiser on the wall.
items.why: The Climbing Doctor's dynamic primer mirrors climbing positions better than long static stretches before activity.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: flags, rotations and tendon glides only. Ages 9–12: full set, skip Rose Move if confusing. Ages 12+ and Ages 14+: full set before harder sessions.
items.risk: Smooth controlled motion only—no ballistic bouncing; stop any movement that hurts; keep the group off the mats under climbers.

items.name: Ankle Rocks
items.setup: Floor space beside a wall, away from fall zones; about 8 minutes.
steps: Stand facing a wall with one foot a hand's length away. Push the knee forward toward the wall while keeping the heel flat on the floor; 10 rocks per side.
Do 12 slow calf raises: rise onto the toes, then lower all the way down.
Calf stretch, 30 seconds per side: hands on the wall, back leg straight, heel down.
Repeat the set once more.
items.why: Stiff ankles limit high steps, heel hooks and smearing. A short routine keeps the range that footwork depends on.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: knee-to-wall rocks only, counted aloud. Ages 9–12: add the calf raises. Ages 12+ and 14+: move the foot a little further from the wall as range improves, and measure the distance every few weeks to see your own progress.
items.risk: Heel stays down on every rock; if it lifts, move the foot closer. Slow, controlled calf raises with no bouncing. Stop any move that causes pain.

items.name: Open Book Twists
items.setup: Mats away from the wall; a rolled towel or block for each climber.
steps: Lie on one side with the top knee bent to 90 degrees and resting on the block, both arms straight in front, palms together.
Open the top arm like a book toward the floor behind you, following it with your eyes. Keep the top knee pressed down so the twist comes from the upper back, not the hips.
Hold 1–2 seconds and return; 10–15 per side.
Then kneel in child's pose, one hand behind the head, and turn that elbow toward the ceiling, 10 per side.
items.why: Rotation through the mid-back lets climbers reach behind them, stem in corners and turn into drop knees without the shoulders and lower back doing all the work.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: call it opening a book and count pages (reps). Ages 9–12: add the child's pose twist. Older groups: use it as a warm-up or at the end of a session.
items.risk: Slow and pain-free; don't force the arm to the floor. If the top knee lifts, the hips are rolling, so press it back down.

items.name: Leg Swings
items.setup: A wall or rail to hold for balance, with space to swing a leg and nobody in front or behind.
steps: Hold the wall. Swing one leg forward and back 15 times, a little higher each swing.
Face the wall and swing the same leg side to side 15 times.
Switch legs, then repeat the whole set once more.
Keep swings relaxed and the hips square.
items.why: Active movement warms the hips, hamstrings and inner thighs for high steps and stems, which suits a pre-climb warm-up better than long static stretches.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: swing like a pendulum and count to 10. Ages 9–12 and up: higher swings as the body warms, still relaxed.
items.risk: Space each climber so legs can't hit anyone. Relaxed swings only; forced kicks are how hamstrings get strained. Hips stay square.

items.name: Standing Hip Circles
items.setup: Floor space next to a wall for balance.
steps: Stand on one leg beside the wall.
Lift the other knee to hip height and draw 10 slow, big circles in one direction, then 10 the other way.
Switch legs, then repeat once more.
Progress by taking the balance hand off the wall.
items.why: Slow big circles wake up the hips and keep their range before high steps and drop knees.
items.variations: Ages 3–6: draw a big rainbow with the knee. Ages 6–9: count circles aloud. Older groups: bigger circles with no hand on the wall.
