items.risk: Stand tall and don't lean away to get the knee higher. Keep a clear arm's length between climbers.

items.name: Butterfly Stretch
items.setup: Mats away from the wall.
steps: Sit up tall with the soles of the feet together and let the knees drop out to the sides.
Hold the feet and gently draw them toward you until a mild stretch shows up in the inner thighs.
Hold 30–45 seconds, relax for 15, repeat 3–5 times.
To deepen, lean forward from the hips with a straight back.
items.why: Inner thighs get used for drop knees, wide stems and high feet but are rarely stretched.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: flap like a butterfly, then hold still. Older groups: sit on the edge of a cushion if the lower back is tight, and draw the heels a little closer rather than forcing the knees down.
items.risk: Never bounce or push the knees down with the hands. Let them drop under their own weight. Stop at the first sign of sharp pain.

items.name: Slow Shoulder Circles
items.setup: Open floor space with arm's length around each climber.
steps: Stand tall and make a tight fist to keep the body still.
Raise one straight arm in front, up past the ear, then rotate it back and down behind you as far as it goes without twisting the body.
Take about 10 seconds per circle; 3 circles in each direction per arm.
Repeat the set once more, making the circle smaller wherever the shoulder feels stuck or pinches.
items.why: Very slow, biggest-possible circles take the shoulder through its whole range before pulling and reaching.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: count to 10 per circle and watch the ribs stay still. Older groups: bigger circles as range returns.
items.risk: Go slowly and don't push through a pinch; make the circle smaller there. A shoulder that stays stuck for weeks should be checked by a physiotherapist.

items.name: Push-Up Plus
items.setup: Mats away from the wall.
steps: Start in a push-up position (knees down is fine).
Do a push-up. At the top with straight elbows, keep pushing the floor away so the upper back rounds slightly and the shoulder blades spread apart.
Let the blades come back together and lower into the next rep.
10–15 reps, up to 3 sets, with a minute's rest between sets.
items.why: The extra push trains the serratus anterior, the muscle that holds the shoulder blade flat against the ribs when reaching overhead.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: knees down, 8–10 reps. Older groups: full push-ups, then add a short pause at the top of each plus; hands on an unstable surface only with coach approval.
items.risk: Bodyweight only. Keep the body in one line from head to knees or heels, elbows tucked, shoulders away from the ears. Stop if a shoulder hurts.

items.name: Auto-Belay Clip-In Routine
items.setup: One auto-belay lane with the gym flag or barrier in place; harnesses on; a coach at the base of each lane.
steps: Self-check the harness: waist above the hips, snug, buckles locked or doubled back per the harness design.
Pull a short section of auto-belay webbing out and let it retract (retraction / function test). If it does not retract, stop and call staff.
Open the auto-locking carabiner, clip it to the belay loop only (not both hard points), gate facing away from the body, and confirm it locks.
Say out loud: “Clipped and locked.” Coach or buddy confirms before the barrier comes down and climbing starts.
items.why: ABC Walls and TRUBLUE both treat a repeated harness check plus retraction test plus locked clip as the habit that prevents climbing unclipped—the main human-error failure mode on auto belays.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 4–6: coach performs the clip and the child names each step (“harness, pull, clip, lock”). Ages 6–9: child clips under coach hands-on supervision; coach still gives the go signal. Ages 9–12 and older: full self-routine, then a partner or coach double-check.
items.risk: Real auto-belay use is induction- and staff-gated at every gym. Nobody climbs until a coach confirms the clip. Keep the physical barrier up until the check is done. Never invent gym-specific carabiner steps—follow the unit in front of you.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays
Gym auto-belay induction or coach-led intro

items.name: Auto-Belay Retraction Test
items.setup: Auto-belay lane; climbers harnessed; coach demonstrates once.
steps: Before clipping, pull the webbing down about arm’s length and release it so it retracts with a clear tug.
After clipping to the belay loop, pull down again and feel the tug on the harness (“double check”).
If the webbing fails to retract, or the tug is missing, unclip if already clipped, step away, and get staff.
items.why: ABC’s “double check before you climb” pairs a visual harness check with a physical retraction test so climbers feel the system working before they leave the ground.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 4–6: coach pulls while the child watches and says “tug!” Older: make the post-clip tug part of every single ascent, even after many climbs in a row (complacency is the failure mode).
items.risk: A failed retraction means do not climb that lane. Staff decide whether the unit is taken out of service.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays

items.name: Auto-Belay Lowering Position
items.setup: Easy auto-belay route; clear landing path; coach at the base.
steps: From a short height (under about 2 m on first tries), practise the descend position: hips back, feet flat on the wall, hands light.
Call “lowering” (or the gym’s word), let the device take weight, and walk feet-first down the wall.
Land with soft knees, walk backward out of the lane about 2 m, then unclip only when both feet are on the ground and the coach says so.
items.why: Campaspe Downs auto-belay SOP has climbers practise the sat/abseil descend position low before full-height climbs, and TRUBLUE requires feet-first descent with a clear path.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 4–6: only the low practise height, coach-controlled. Ages 6–9: add a mid-route pause, then continue the lower. Ages 9+: combine with a full-height climb on an easy color.
items.risk: Do not start a descent from above the device. Clear the path of people and gear. Unclip only on the ground under staff control for young climbers.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays

items.name: Auto-Belay Lane Boundaries
items.setup: Walk the auto-belay area as a group before anyone climbs.
steps: Point out the marked belay zone / lane edges and the flag or barrier at the base.
Explain: climb only inside the lane; never beside or above the device; never faster than the webbing can retract.
Have each climber walk the “out of lane” path on the floor (without climbing) so they can see where not to go.
items.why: TRUBLUE’s operating tips and ABC’s barrier guidance both treat lane discipline and the physical flag as core risk-management controls, not optional etiquette.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 4–6: “red zone / green zone” floor tape. Older: climbers teach the next group the lane edges.
items.risk: If slack appears because a climber outclimbs retraction, slow down or stop. Coach watches sight lines the whole block.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays

items.name: Staff-Controlled First Auto Belay
items.setup: One easy auto-belay; only the coach clips and unclips; waiting climbers behind a clear line.
steps: Coach fits/checks harness, clips the carabiner, does the retraction tug, and gives a clear “climb” signal.
Climber goes only as high as they choose; coach can call “stop” for a reach game or technique cue a few metres up.
Lower with the practised sit-back position; coach unclips on the ground.
items.why: NICAS Clip starts auto-belay pathways from about age 5 with staff-led sessions, and Campaspe SOP keeps clipping/unclipping instructor-controlled for many youth groups.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 4–6: two short ascents, high-five the star height they pick. Ages 6–9: add naming one hold color at the top before lowering.
items.risk: Maximum people in the climbing area per gym SOP (often 1–2). Only staff clip. Permission before every ascent.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays

items.name: Auto-Belay Pace Control
items.setup: Easy auto-belay route; coach watches for slack loops in the webbing.
steps: Climb at a steady pace. If the webbing shows a slack loop, freeze, let it catch up, then continue slower.
At the top, pause, check the descent path, then lower feet-first.
Repeat one more lap focusing on never creating slack.
items.why: TRUBLUE and youth auto-belay SOPs both flag climbing faster than retraction as a primary operating error.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 6–9: coach calls “slow” / “go” to set pace. Ages 12+: personal-best “zero slack” laps on an easy endurance color.
items.risk: If slack appears, stop climbing up until it retracts. Stay inside the lane.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays

items.name: Downclimb to Auto-Belay Unclip
items.setup: Easy auto-belay on vertical or slab; coach at the base.
steps: Climb to a chosen mid-height mark, then downclimb holds until both feet are on the ground while still clipped.
Only when weight is fully on the feet and the coach confirms, unclip and reattach the carabiner to the gate/parking point.
Walk backward out of the lane.
items.why: Pairs downclimbing skill with the hard rule that unclipping happens on the ground after a controlled finish, reinforcing TRUBLUE’s reattach-on-landing protocol.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Younger: downclimb only the last two metres, then lower the rest. Older: full downclimb of a short easy route as an endurance finisher.
items.risk: Never unclip at height. Coach watches the unclip. Keep the landing path clear.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays

items.name: Auto-Belay Reach Games Low
items.setup: Auto-belay; targets or named holds only a few metres up; coach-controlled clip-in for younger climbers.
steps: Climb only to the low target zone (a few metres).
Complete a technique task: touch three colors, quiet feet for five moves, or flag once.
Lower with the practised position. Personal completion—no ranking.
items.why: Campaspe SOP recommends reaching games and technique exercises a few metres off the ground before exposure to full height shapes movement habits.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 4–6: touch the blue hold and come down. Ages 6–9: silent feet to the mark. Ages 9–12: add a rest-shake at the mark.
items.risk: Keep early volume low. Staff control clip-in for the youngest. Clear lane.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays
Staff-Controlled First Auto Belay or Auto-Belay Clip-In Routine

items.name: Top-Rope Route Preview
items.setup: A top-rope route the climber has not done today; belay pair ready but still on the ground.
steps: From outside the fall line, point to each handhold in order and name rests or awkward sections.
Say the start commands only after the partner check.
Climb the plan; after lowering, name one thing that matched and one that changed.
items.why: Route preview before leaving the ground is standard rope practice and matches how Momentum focus drills and lead clinics ask climbers to think before they pull on.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: point only the first five holds. Ages 12+: time a short observation period like a comp preview, still personal.
items.risk: Stand clear of other climbers’ fall lines while reading. Partner check before every climb.

items.name: Top-Rope Rest Hunt
items.setup: Moderate-easy top-rope route with at least two obvious rest stances; attentive belayer.
steps: On the ground, mark two likely rests.
Climb, stop at each rest, straight-arm shake one hand, then the other.
Lower and redraw the rest map if a better stance appeared.
items.why: Finding rests on rope terrain is how climbers turn endurance routes into managed efforts; it builds on shake-out skill already used on boulders.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: one rest only, big jug. Ages 12+: plan rests before leaving the ground, then test the plan.
items.risk: Belayer keeps a snug top rope at rests. Climber chooses when to leave a rest.
prereqs: Astronaut Lowering or equivalent lowering position

items.name: Push-Off Fall Practice
items.setup: Slightly overhanging or clean vertical top-rope; experienced belayer; climber chooses height.
steps: Climb to a comfortable height on a snug top rope.
Bend the legs, push off the wall, relax the arms, and land back with soles of the feet, knees soft, feet about shoulder-width.
Repeat, pushing a little harder only while the climber still looks and sounds relaxed.
items.why: Rock & Sun stage 1 builds falling skill inside the climber’s comfort zone before any lead falls; Prowess episode 1 similarly starts with controlled top-rope slumps the climber chooses.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: tiny push-offs only, coach belay. Ages 9–12: add a calm breath before each push. Ages 12+: progress later to sideways pendulum comfort, still on top rope.
items.risk: Belayer manages slack deliberately. Clear fall line. Climber decides when to stop. Prefer slightly overhanging terrain so the body swings into space, not into panels.
prereqs: Comfort sitting on the rope (Astronaut Lowering)

items.name: Pendulum Comfort on Top Rope
items.setup: Top rope with space to move sideways; belayer and coach agree the swing arc is clear of people and features.
steps: From a mid-height stance, walk or shuffle sideways on the wall until a gentle pendulum starts, then return.
When ready, add a small push at the end of the swing so the landing uses feet and bent knees.
Stop while it still feels manageable; talk about what the body did.
items.why: Rock & Sun stage 2 specifically trains sideways falls and pendulum landings that real rope climbing produces when a climber is off the fall line.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: tiny side steps only with coach belay. Ages 14+: slightly larger swings on clean overhanging terrain.
items.risk: Coach-run only. Clear the entire swing arc. No King-Swing-sized offsets unless that separate activity is planned with full clearance.

items.name: Clip-and-Let-Go on Top Rope
items.setup: Top rope on a route with visible bolt hangers or draws beside the line; skilled belayer; climber already comfortable with push-off falls.
steps: Climb to a draw, touch it, and let go with minimal hesitation while arms stay relaxed.
Repeat at successive draws. Belayer starts snug and only adds a little slack when the climber asks and looks relaxed.
End on a fall the climber would gladly repeat.
items.why: Rock & Sun stage 3 uses touch-and-let-go on top rope to read hesitation and body tension before any lead fall ladder.
items.variations: Keep it to two or three touches per session. If hesitation returns, drop back to Push-Off Fall Practice.
items.risk: Top rope only in this activity. Belayer skill matters. Slightly overhanging, clear terrain. Climber-led progression.

items.name: Progressive Top-Rope Slump
items.setup: Slightly overhanging top rope; climber brought to about the fourth bolt height and rested on the rope; belayer holds steady slack.
steps: From hanging on the rope, pull onto the wall and slump back without the belayer changing slack.
Pull on, make one move, and let go, returning near the same height.
Add moves only while the climber chooses; finish on a comfortable slump.
items.why: Prowess Climbing Coaching’s lead-fall episode 1 builds falling comfort on top rope with climber-chosen height before true lead falls.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: coach belay, fewer reps. Ages 12+: peer belay only if both are certified and a coach backs up.
items.risk: Fatigue raises stress—stop early if form or mood drops. Climber alone picks the biggest slump.

items.name: Take and Lower Sequence
items.setup: Top rope; belay pair; coach listening.
steps: At a rest or the top, climber calls “take” (or gym word); belayer takes rope tight and answers.
Climber sits, confirms weight on the rope, then calls “lower.”
Belayer lowers at a steady pace while climber keeps feet on the wall; finish with “off belay” / gym end calls only when standing on the ground.
items.why: Climb’s lead syllabus and every top-rope program treat clear take/lower communication as non-negotiable rope risk management.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: “ready / hold me / going down” simplified words matching the gym. Ages 9+: add “slack” and “that’s me” where the gym uses them.
items.risk: Always use the gym’s standard commands. Belayer’s brake hand never leaves the brake strand. Staff supervise uncertified belayers.

items.name: Belay Stance Practice
items.setup: Ground school rope through a low anchor or coach-held climber end; backup belayer; tube device or ABD per gym policy.
steps: Set an athletic stance, facing the wall, brake hand on the brake strand.
Practise taking in and paying out while keeping the stance; partner gives gentle body-weight tugs with a backup.
Name what changes for a heavier or lighter climber (stance, attention, possible ground anchor per gym rules).
items.why: Climb’s syllabus and GVSU lead lesson both list belayer positioning and weight-difference management as explicit learning objectives.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: stance and take-in only, coach as backup. Ages 12+: add soft-catch discussion for future lead belay, still ground-loaded.
items.risk: No live lead belaying until gym certification. Backup belayer required. Follow the gym’s device policy.

items.name: Figure-8 Dressing Lab
items.setup: Spare practice ropes; photos or coach-tied models of dressed and messy figure-8 follow-throughs.
steps: Tie a figure-8 follow-through through both tie-in points on a harness (practice harness on the ground).
Dress it: parallel strands, no big crosses, fist-length or gym-standard tail, optional stopper if the gym requires it.
Partner counts the five pairs of strands and traces the rope path before a coach confirms.
items.why: Climb’s day-1 tying block and Momentum knot practice both treat a correctly dressed figure-8 as the foundation of every partner check.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 6–9: finish one correct knot with heavy coach help; do not rush. Ages 9+: add spotting common errors (short tail, only one tie-in point, undressed twists).
items.risk: Practice knots never replace a coach check on a real tie-in. Nobody climbs on an unchecked knot.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays

items.name: Harness Parts Callout
items.setup: Harnesses on the mat; coach points, climbers name.
steps: Point to waist belt, leg loops, belay loop, tie-in points, gear loops, buckle.
Climbers repeat names, then swap: climber points, peer names.
End by showing the only clip-in point used for the auto-belay carabiner or belay device (belay loop) and the two tie-in points for the rope.
items.why: ABC auto-belay induction and Climb’s gear overview both start with harness attachment points because wrong clip-in points create serious loading problems.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 3–4: waist and leg loops only, with a parent. Ages 4–6: add belay loop. Ages 9+: add “why not clip both hard points” (tri-axial loading idea in kid words).
items.risk: Gear-loop carabiners are never load-bearing. Coach confirms every real clip-in.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays

items.name: Clipping Stance Finder
items.setup: Quickdraws on a low bolt board or first bolts of an easy lead line used only for ground/low practice under coach control; or mock-lead setup.
steps: Before clipping, set feet and a solid hand so the clip hand is free.
Practise clipping from that stance with either hand; reset if the body barn-doors.
Name a “good” and “stretched” clip stance on the same bolt.
items.why: Climb’s clipping block and SNCS Level 2 both emphasize finding a stable clipping position before the rope goes near the draw—rushing clips causes errors.
items.variations: Ages 12+: on mock lead with top-rope backup.
items.risk: No live leading until certified. Coach checks every practice clip pattern.

items.name: Back-Clip Spotting Board
items.setup: Ground clipping board with several draws; coach presets a mix of correct clips and back-clips.
steps: Climbers walk the board and mark each clip correct or back-clipped.
For each back-clip, explain the rope path (rope should run from the wall/bolt side out toward the climber in the gym’s taught orientation) and fix it.
Retest with new presets.
items.why: Back-clipping is a named failure mode in Climb’s syllabus, GVSU lead objectives, Mazamas sport leader day 2, and SNCS Level 2 assessment standards.
items.variations: Ages 14+: timed personal accuracy set—count your own correct fixes, not against peers.
items.risk: Ground practice only. Agree the gym’s rope-direction teaching model before debating edge cases.

items.name: Z-Clip Recognition Drill
items.setup: Two draws on a board or low wall; coach demos grabbing rope from below the last clip.
steps: Demo a correct clip: rope taken from near the harness/knot side above the last clipped draw.
Demo a Z-clip: rope taken from below the previous draw into the next, making a Z and heavy drag.
Climbers practise the correct hand path slowly, then identify coach-made Z mistakes.
items.why: Z-clipping is called out across lead syllabi (Climb, Camp5 Lead Wall Course, SNCS) because it creates drag and a hazardous rope path.
items.variations: Start exaggerated and slow. Later, add the cue “grab rope close to the knot.”
items.risk: Ground or mock-lead only. Fix any Z before anyone climbs higher in a mock setting.

items.name: Rope-Behind-Leg Awareness
items.setup: Mock-lead or low lead practice with top-rope backup; coach watches rope and legs.
steps: Climb a few moves with a trailing rope and notice when the rope runs behind a leg or thigh.
Practise moving the rope in front of the legs before the next clip.
Talk through what a fall with the rope behind the leg can do (flip potential) in age-appropriate words.
items.why: Climb’s clipping block explicitly asks “what happens when you put your leg behind the rope?”—a standard lead risk-management teaching point.
items.variations: Demo on the ground with a rope around a volunteer’s leg (gentle, no pulling). On mock lead, coach calls “rope” when it drifts behind a leg.
items.risk: Mock lead / top-rope backup until lead certified. Coach present.

items.name: Rope-Drag Zigzag Demo
items.setup: Mock-lead draws that can be clipped in a zigzag and a straighter line; climbers feel pull by hand on the ground first.
steps: Clip a zigzag path on the board or mock draws and pull rope through—notice the drag.
Reclip a straighter path and compare the pull.
On an easy mock lead, choose draws that keep the rope closer to a straight line when the route allows.
items.why: Rope drag from zigzags is a core lead efficiency and risk topic in lead courses and matches the existing Rope Drag vocabulary already in the library.
items.variations: Ground pulls only for a first session. Later: extend with quickdraw gate orientation so the rope runs clean.
items.risk: Practice under coach control. Do not fight extreme drag by yanking—fix and reclimb the clip plan.

items.name: Gate Orientation Drill
items.setup: Loose quickdraws and a bolt hanger board.
steps: Show dogbone, bolt-end carabiner, rope-end carabiner.
Hang draws so gates face away from the likely fall / travel direction per gym teaching (often alternating or gate away from expected movement).
Climbers hang a set of draws and a partner checks gate direction before any rope is introduced.
items.why: SNCS Level 2 and Climb’s quickdraw anatomy blocks treat gate/spine orientation as part of correct protection setup, not a trivia detail.
items.variations: Ages 12+: climbers hang practice draws on a mock route.
items.risk: Practice hardware only. Real lead walls follow gym rules about pre-hung and climber-placed draws.

items.name: First Three Clips Focus
items.setup: Easy lead line with top-rope backup or auto-belay backup per Climb’s mock-lead model; coach belay for first sessions.
steps: Discuss why the first clips matter most for ground-fall risk management.
On mock lead, practise calm, solid clips on bolts 1–3 only, then lower.
Repeat until those three clips look identical and unhurried.
items.why: SNCS and GVSU materials highlight ground-fall risk before enough clips are in; Climb uses auto-belay-backed mock leading on day 1 for exactly this kind of deliberate practice.
items.variations: Use stick-clip for bolt 1 if the gym teaches it. Only advance to higher bolts after low clips are automatic.
items.risk: Backup belay required. No live lead without certification and coach approval. Steep, clean lines preferred.

items.name: Mock Lead with Auto-Belay Backup
items.setup: Lead route with an auto-belay (or top rope) as the true belay; a second rope or the lead rope used only to practise clipping draws.
steps: Partner-check the real belay system first (auto-belay or top rope).
Climb while clipping the practice lead rope into draws; coach watches for back-clips, Z-clips, and rope-behind-leg.
At the top or a chosen height, stop, discuss clips, and lower on the real belay.
items.why: Climb’s lead syllabus schedules mock leading on day 1—lead movement with an auto-belay backup—before day 2 live lead and fall practice.
items.variations: Pre-hung draws first (pinkpoint-style practice), then place draws if the gym allows. Add a coach checklist card: gate, direction, Z, legs, stance.
items.risk: The backup system is the real belay—treat it with a full clip-in or top-rope partner check every time. Practice rope is not the catch.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays
Auto-Belay Clip-In Routine or top-rope Partner Check

items.name: Lead Fall Below the Draw
items.setup: Steep, clean lead terrain; climber lead-certified or on a clinic rope with instructor belay; start at least ~2 m below a clipped draw; clear fall zone.
steps: From a four-point easy stance below the clipped draw, breathe, make a small upward move, and let go with relaxed arms.
Land with eyes toward the feet/wall, knees soft, feet apart; optional hand on rope near the knot per Rock & Sun cues.
Increase fall length only when climber and coach agree body language still looks relaxed.
items.why: Rock & Sun stage 4 builds lead falling from below the draw before chin-above or feet-above progressions; Camp5 and Climb keep lead fall practice inside structured clinics.
items.variations: Ages 12+: instructor belay first. Ages 14+: peer lead belay only if both passed the gym lead test and a coach supervises.
items.risk: High consequence. Certified lead belayer, coach present, overhanging clear terrain, climber-chosen progress. Stop early if tension or shrieking returns.
prereqs: Clip-and-Let-Go on Top Rope or Progressive Top-Rope Slump

items.name: Soft-Catch Concept Lab
items.setup: Whiteboard or demo rope; no live falls required in the lab itself.
steps: Define a hard catch (sudden stop, belayer static) and a soft catch (belayer moves with the fall / managed slack) in gym-appropriate terms.
Discuss when a soft catch helps (higher lead falls on steep ground) and when it does not (low to the ground, ledges, swinging into hazards).
Role-play the words belayer and climber use before a planned practice fall.
items.why: Climb’s falling discussion and GVSU objectives explicitly contrast soft and hard catches and weight differences before climbers practise catching lead falls.
items.variations: Add a supervised ground-weight demo with a backup belayer if the gym allows. Pair with Lead Fall Below the Draw on a later day—not the same hour for brand-new belayers.
items.risk: Concepts first; live soft catches only with certified lead belayers under coach oversight.

items.name: Lead Age-Readiness Talk
items.setup: Seated group; gym lead policy printed or summarized by coach.
steps: Review common prerequisites from published courses: solid top-rope belay, comfortable moderate top-rope climbing, minimum ages often ~12–13 (some programs 10–12 only with a participating adult).
Each climber writes two skills they already have and one they still need (clipping, falling comfort, belay stance, endurance).
Set a process goal for the block—not a deadline to “get lead card.”
items.why: Published lead courses set age and skill gates (often about 12–13+). A short readiness talk keeps ages 9–12 honest about waiting, and helps ages 12+ / 14+ map the gym’s real prerequisites without rushing into lead.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: readiness talk only—no mock lead or live lead; focus on what still needs practice on top rope. Ages 12+ and Ages 14+: map the gym lead-test rubric and set process goals. Ages 14+: map the gym’s exact test rubric.
items.risk: Do not pressure early lead. Gym policy always comes first over any curriculum sample.

items.name: Commands Clarity Ladder
items.setup: Pairs across a noisy gym space but still able to hear; no climbing required.
steps: Caller says a command at conversation volume; partner echoes the exact gym response.
Increase distance step by step, keeping words crisp—not shouted garbage.
Finish with the full start-up chain and the take/lower chain.
items.why: Clear commands are required in Climb’s belay protocols and SNCS assessment standards; practising clarity away from the wall prevents mumbled calls on real climbs.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 4–6: two-word gym baby commands only. Ages 12+: add lead calls (slack, clipping, falling).
items.risk: Use only the gym’s command set so class words match floor staff.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays

items.name: Partner Check Point-Trace
items.setup: Belay pairs fully dressed to climb; coach watches one pair at a time.
steps: Checker points to and says: harness buckles, figure-8 through both tie-ins and dressed, belay device on belay loop, locker locked, rope-end knot if required, loose clothing/hair clear.
Swap roles. Climber does not pull on until both have finished.
Coach asks one surprise question (“show me the brake strand”) before go.
items.why: Extends the existing Partner Check habit with a mandatory point-and-trace motor pattern; Climb and ABC both stress that checks fail when they become waved gestures.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: fewer items, coach completes the list. Lead day add-ons: backup knot, lead end identified, draws racked.
items.risk: No check, no climb. Uncertified belayers always have a staff backup.

items.name: Paying Out and Taking In
items.setup: Ground school with a moving partner walking away/toward the belayer; backup belayer; gym-approved device.
steps: As the partner walks away, pay out smooth slack without locking the device early (especially ABD/Grigri awareness).
As the partner walks in, take in quickly while the brake hand stays on the brake strand.
Name errors: short-roping (too tight) and too much slack.
items.why: GVSU and SNCS lead-belay objectives call out smooth slack payout, rapid take-in, and avoiding short-roping or premature ABD lock-up.
items.variations: Tube device and ABD in separate turns if the gym teaches both. Add a sudden sit by the partner (with backup) to practise a catch stance.
items.risk: Backup always. No unsupervised belaying. Device-specific techniques must match staff teaching.

items.name: Top-Rope Endurance Laps
items.setup: Easy top-rope routes well below limit; belay pairs; partner check every relisten/re-tie.
steps: Climb an easy route at a talk pace, lower or downclimb, rest briefly, repeat for a set number of personal laps.
Focus on straight arms and shake-outs rather than grade.
Log your own lap count; try to match it next week with equal or better form.
items.why: Momentum’s two-in-a-rows and disco climbing show how rope volume builds endurance when the grade stays easy and checks stay strict.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: two climbs total. Ages 9–12: disco style to bolt 3, downclimb, repeat. Ages 12+: continuous easy laps with planned rests.
items.risk: Partner check every time someone ties in again. Stop when form breaks. Brake hand rules never relax with fatigue.

items.name: Auto-Belay Endurance Colors
items.setup: Easy auto-belay colors; full clip-in routine every lap; coach floor-walking.
steps: Complete the clip-in routine, climb an easy color at pace-control speed, lower, unclip on the ground, rest.
Repeat for a personal target number of quality laps.
If complacency shows (rushed clip), freeze the session and redo the routine slowly.
items.why: TRUBLUE markets auto belays for endurance training, and ABC warns that experienced climbers fail when they rush the clip after many laps—so endurance blocks must keep the routine sacred.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 6–9: two laps. Ages 12+: longer sets still below pump-out.
items.risk: Full double-check every lap. Staff watch for unclipped starts. No outclimbing retraction.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays

items.name: Quickdraw Anatomy Sort
items.setup: Disassembled practice draws (or labeled photos if hardware cannot be borrowed).
steps: Sort: bolt-end carabiner, rope-end carabiner, dogbone/sewn sling.
Reassemble correctly and explain which end usually has the bent gate in many gym draws.
Partner checks the rebuild.
items.why: Climb’s day-1 gear overview and SNCS equipment blocks require climbers to know draw anatomy before they clip them on lead.
items.variations: Photo cards for gyms that will not hand out loose hardware. Add a worn and retired sling discussion for older teens.
items.risk: Practice gear only; nothing with unknown history goes back on a climb without staff approval.

items.name: Closed-System Rope End
items.setup: Belay ropes with enough end to tie the gym’s required end knot.
steps: Show why a rope-end knot (barrel / double overhand, per gym) stops the rope from running through the device.
Each belayer ties and dresses the end knot, partner checks.
Add the end knot to the partner-check list out loud.
items.why: Partner-check lists in youth programs and lead clinics routinely include the rope-end knot as part of a closed belay system.
items.variations: Some gyms use rope-end bags or sewn ends—teach the local method, not a generic substitute.
items.risk: Follow gym policy exactly. A missing end knot is a no-climb item.
prereqs: Knot Practice or Figure-8 Dressing Lab

items.name: Backup Belayer Habit
items.setup: Top-rope team of three: climber, belayer, backup; coach assigns roles.
steps: Backup stands ready to catch the brake strand without interfering.
Run a short climb with coach watching the belayer’s brake hand and the backup’s attention.
Rotate roles. Only certified or coach-approved belayers take the primary role.
items.why: Ground-school progressions and youth SOPs keep a backup until climbers pass a belay test; the habit belongs in class even after some kids certify.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: backup is always a coach. Ages 12+: trained peers backup under coach eyes.
items.risk: Backup does not mean unsupervised. Gym certification still gates primary belaying.
